name: VTDigger
title: Rink on the brink: Barre makes last-minute ice rink repairs, but the arena’s future is uncertain
description:
For one local high school coach, the rink holds three generations of family history.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Rink on the brink: Barre makes last-minute ice rink repairs, but the arena’s future is uncertain.
text:
The B.O.R. Barre Outdoor Recreation arena on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. Photo by Erin Petenko/VTDigger

BARRE — As a boy visiting his grandfather in Barre, Brian Wilkin could see the arches of the city’s new ice arena as he walked down the hill. His grandfather lived next to the arena, and Wilkin understood what the new building meant: He would be able to play hockey in his own hometown.
And he did. So did his father. Eventually, his daughter did, too.
Now Wilkin, the Spaulding High School girls hockey coach, is wondering how his players could cope without the rink that has given three generations of his family a place to play.
“It’s going to be hard to keep a group of kids together when you don’t have a home,” Wilkin said.
Needed emergency repairs could keep Barre’s BOR Arena open this winter after city officials announced last week that failures in the pipes beneath the ice would force it to close for the season. 
Even if repairs save this season, however, Barre must still confront an aging arena in need of more work.
“I think we got a little complacent and figured, ‘OK, if there’s a problem, we’ll just fix it,’” said Barre Mayor Thom Lauzon. “And it’s time to take a real hard look at replacing the system. I don’t want to go through this again.”
For Wilkin’s players, the arena is more than a place to practice and compete. It is where they watch movies, train off the ice and spend time together. Those hours help a roster become a team.
And while Wilkin said he has promising young players coming in this year, a prolonged shutdown could make it harder to build that camaraderie.
The uncertainty extends beyond his team. Spaulding’s boys also practice and play at the arena, which hosts youth hockey, figure skating and public skating. In summer, the ice gives way to turf for soccer, lacrosse and walking.
“We use it daily for practices, it’s used for all of our games,” said Derek Cipriano, Spaulding’s director of athletics and activities. “It’s kind of like our home base of operations.”
Teams have worked around trouble with the ice before. Last year, Wilkin’s players finished their final week of the season at other nearby arenas after a smaller break in the system.
Barre has also provided ice for others. U-32 High School’s team has borrowed the arena toward the end of its season when its home rink converts to turf.
But a short disruption is different from losing an entire season at home. Cipriano said “there isn’t a ton of ice time available” at other facilities. 
“If the BOR doesn’t have ice, we’ll be having some really early morning practices,” he said. “We’re trying to piece together where we can fit our schedule in.” 
Trouble below
The rink’s history began with a much more visible failure.
Its roof collapsed during construction in 1972, forcing the city to rebuild, according to a 2015 Times Argus account. The arena eventually opened in 1974 at a cost of $400,000. Half came from the federal Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, whose initials supplied the building’s name.
This time, the trouble is underneath the ice. City officials said last week that the pipe system had developed several major problems, prompting the closure announcement.
Four local contractors — Trym Chouinard, Ed Patterson, Colby LaPerle and Jeff Gould — volunteered their time to attempt emergency repairs. By Tuesday morning, Lauzon said, he had heard they had repaired the first loop of cooling pipes.
“What they’re going to do over the next two or three days is they’re going to repair the leaks, and hopefully we don’t have any more issues with it,” he said.
Beyond that immediate work, Lauzon said the city needs to consider a more comprehensive overhaul. Borrowing about $2 million for repairs would require annual payments of roughly $130,000, he estimated.
That is about as much as the city brings in each year from ice rentals, according to the mayor. Keeping the arena open, if Barre can, is worth doing, he said. “(We’ll) have no net revenue, but we’ll have a nice rink,” he said. 
For Wilkin, the building’s value also lies in what happens between practices and games: the movies, the conversations and the time his players spend together in the rink where he once played.
It is where, as he put it, they “come together as a team.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: USDA secretary urges states to allow on-road dyed diesel
description: U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said Tuesday in Iowa that she is urging state governors to follow the president’s move to suspend penalties on the unrestricted use of dyed diesel, a tax-exempt fuel typically allowed in off-road machinery only.  President Donald Trump announced Monday evening at a rally in Nebraska he would authorize highway […]
text:
President Donald Trump authorized highway use of dyed diesel fuel and some states are following suit.  (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital dispatch)U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said Tuesday in Iowa that she is urging state governors to follow the president’s move to suspend penalties on the unrestricted use of dyed diesel, a tax-exempt fuel typically allowed in off-road machinery only. 
President Donald Trump announced Monday evening at a rally in Nebraska he would authorize highway use of dyed diesel fuel and defer the federal excise tax on the fuel to provide relief from the steep diesel prices which have hit record highs of more than $6 per gallon, nationally. 
The move from Trump followed actions from several states, like Ohio, to suspend state fuel taxes or to allow dyed diesel fuel. After Trump’s Monday-night executive order, more states, including Iowa, have leveraged similar state-level suspensions. 
Rollins, speaking with reporters at a stop in Iowa Tuesday, said she is “on the phone constantly with other governors, trying to get them to do the same.” 
Rollins said 13 governors, including Democratic Gov. Josh Stein in North Carolina, have followed suit. 
“I’m working on a lot of the other Democrat governors, saying … this will really help your constituents and your farmers.” 

About dyed diesel
Dyed diesel fuel is a tax-exempt diesel fuel used in off-road equipment for farming, construction and heating. The diesel is dyed red so that law enforcement can identify the fuel and enforce penalties when it is used on roads. 

According to the executive order from the president, the federal suspension could save drivers as much as $100 per trip to the fuel station. Corn growers from Iowa wrote to Iowa’s congressional delegation in September and asked them to push for federal waivers to use dyed diesel on the road, in addition to calls to stop diesel exports and to release oil from the national reserves. 
Iowa Corn Growers Association President Steve Kuiper said in a statement Tuesday the expanded use of dyed diesel will “help provide financial relief” to farmers “when they need it most during harvest.”
In his announcement Monday evening, Trump said the order would allow “anyone” to purchase red-dyed diesel fuel “for any reason.” Trump’s executive order runs through the end of the calendar year. 
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds’ proclamation Tuesday temporarily suspended penalties on dyed diesel that is used in on-road vehicles hauling agricultural products, like corn, soybeans, hay and fertilizers. The Iowa proclamation runs through Feb. 2, 2027.
“This will lower costs for farmers through the harvest and beyond by opening access to tax-free fuel,” Reynolds said in a statement.
Rollins said Tuesday that in addition to the executive order on dyed diesel, an influx of 100 million barrels of oil from the Group of Seven, or G7, countries have “already” caused the price of diesel to decline. The G7 announcement was made Friday. According to AAA fuel price data, the national average price of diesel was about $0.13 per gallon lower Tuesday than a week prior. 
U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, center, at a farm near Prairie City, Iowa, Oct. 6, 2026, speaking about USDA seed sovereignty program alongside Iowa Reps. Zach Nunn, front left, and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, right. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“There’s a lot of really good things that are being deployed right now,” Rollins said. 
Fuel prices have risen sharply due to the ongoing war in Iran and closures in the Strait of Hormuz, a prominent trade route for products like oil and fertilizer, combined with continued conflict between Russia and Ukraine. 
In his rally speech in Nebraska, Trump said the situation in Iran is “going to be over with very soon.” Rollins echoed the sentiment Tuesday when asked about the war and said the government of Iran “cannot have” a nuclear weapon and that the war was “so important for the future.”
“He has said that we’re moving quickly, that we will and should be out of it very soon,” Rollins said. “When that happens, all of the fuel prices, everything will absolutely go down significantly.” 
Rollins said the current situation “is exactly why” the administration is “working so hard” to increase domestic energy production. 
Rollins, who spoke alongside Iowa Congressman Zach Nunn at an event in Des Moines, said onshoring fuel production doesn’t just mean oil, but also investing in biofuel production.
Rollins said Nunn and the rest of Iowa’s congressional delegation are “the reason” the current administration is considered the most “pro-biofuels administration in history.” Iowa’s delegation have joined other agriculture heavy states in pushing for action on things like access to year-round, nationwide E-15, which advocates say would help farmers and lower prices at the fuel pump. 
U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, another Republican from Iowa, also joined Rollins earlier in the day at a Jasper County farm for an announcement about the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s seed sovereignty program. Miller-Meeks cheered the House-passed bill for E-15 and said the country just needs “that pesky Senate to act.” 
Nunn and Miller-Meeks also spoke about the importance of finalizing 45Z rules, a tax credit for domestically produced biofuel, including sustainable aviation fuel, in bringing down fuel prices. 
Rollins’ visit to Iowa, Trump’s announcement on diesel and individual state actions to lower fuel prices coincides with a competitive upcoming midterm election in which Republicans hope to maintain the majority. Nunn and Miller-Meeks are both seeking reelection and face competitive races in Iowa.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: State GOP leadership relieved at withdrawal of endorsement of Mike Caruso
description: The Republican Party of Palm Beach County has purged ousted Clerk of the Court Mike Caruso, who’s been charged with five felony counts of child molestation, from its list of candidates to support in the midterm elections. Gov. Ron DeSantis, who removed Caruso from office despite him being a close ally, said Tuesday that the […]
text:
Gov. DeSantis signs anti-hate legislation in Jerusalem with GOP Reps. Randy Fine and Mike Caruso. (Via Randy Fine's Twitter page)The Republican Party of Palm Beach County has purged ousted Clerk of the Court Mike Caruso, who’s been charged with five felony counts of child molestation, from its list of candidates to support in the midterm elections.
Gov. Ron DeSantis, who removed Caruso from office despite him being a close ally, said Tuesday that the local party made a mistake by including him in its voter guide.
“And sometimes you just got to do the right thing. I think the right thing in this position is not to be endorsing, you know, a candidate that is that is under those potential very serious charges,” the governor said.
Caruso’s name is still on the Nov. 3 ballot, Alison Novoa, spokesperson for the county supervisor of elections, confirmed. His opponent is Boca Raton City Councilmember Yvette Drucker.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Caruso is running to retain the office to which DeSantis had appointed him.
DeSantis suspended Caruso following his arrest in August. An Orange County trial judge authorized his release on a $160,000 bond, the Orlando Sentinel reported.
“For the record, our Voter Guide originally listed every Republican nominee on the ballot, as we are required to do by Florida Statute. As soon as we were permitted to remove the nominee running for a constitutional office, we did,” the local party said on social media.
“I appreciate the @PalmBeachGOP doing the right thing,” Republican Party of Florida Chair Evan Power wrote on X.
U.S. Sen. Rick Scott wrote on X, “This is disgusting. Mike Caruso should IMMEDIATELY withdraw. The people of Palm Beach deserve better.”
DeSantis said Caruso is entitled to the presumption of innocence but “that does not mean a political party should just support someone by default rather than take a look at the circumstances of the situation.”
He continued: “But from our perspective, for a Republican Party, why would you want to be doing an endorsement under those circumstances?
“I think there were circumstances that warranted his removal from his position, and he had been a state rep, and then had been in the clerk’s office. So, so, so, when I was presented with that, I made the right decision there, and I think that party is fine, but it’s not the end-all, be-all,” the governor said.
“And yes, criminally, you know, the process is going to play out. And he does deserve the presumption of innocence there. But in the political context, to have been removed from office because there was sufficient evidence to do it, to me, you know, that’s enough to say no dice.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas lawmakers begin discussions on state’s budget as election looms
description: Arkansas lawmakers began a monthlong series of state budget discussions Tuesday, with the state military and labor departments fielding questions about how they expect to spend their money next year.  The Joint Budget Committee approved both agencies’ budget proposals with no dissent. The panel will submit each approved budget recommendation to the full Legi[...]
text:
From left: Arkansas Bureau of Legislative Research analyst Blake Smith, Department of Military Chief Financial Officer Diane Worm and Arkansas National Guard Deputy Adjutant General Jeff Wood present the military department's fiscal years 2028 and 2029 budget proposal to state lawmakers on Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas lawmakers began a monthlong series of state budget discussions Tuesday, with the state military and labor departments fielding questions about how they expect to spend their money next year. 
The Joint Budget Committee approved both agencies’ budget proposals with no dissent. The panel will submit each approved budget recommendation to the full Legislature, which begins its regular session in January.
The Department of Labor and Licensing’s proposed budget prompted several questions from the committee because it projected significantly lower spending than the amount of funding requested.
The agency has been “trying to do more with less” and cutting unnecessary spending, Secretary Daryl Bassett said.
“At the same time, though, we need to have a buffer just in case something happens,” he said.
In June, Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders directed cabinet secretaries to “work collaboratively to cut costs” in their departments. Lawmakers have cut individual and corporate income taxes five times in the past five years.

Arkansas Explained: What’s happening with state tax cuts?


Arkansas ended the 2026 fiscal year June 30 with a $655 million budget surplus, nearly $300 million more than the previous year. The state has about $4 billion in reserves.
Sanders is expected to unveil her 2027 balanced budget proposal in late November.
The 2026 budget included a $139 million state employee pay plan meant to increase the starting salaries of hard-to-fill jobs, such as corrections officers and social services workers, to make them competitive with the private sector and increase retention.
The state budget for the current fiscal year, which began July 1, totals $6.7 billion.
The labor department projects a roughly $4 million increase in its expenditures for each of the next two fiscal years compared to the current one because its pay plan increases salaries and benefits by up to 3% annually, chief financial officer Tyler Cain said.
The Department of Military’s budget proposal requests roughly $118 million for each of the next two fiscal years. The request is about $11 million more than the current fiscal year, Bureau of Legislative Research analyst Blake Smith said.
Lawmakers will hear from the Arkansas Department of Health and the Department of Parks, Heritage and Tourism on Wednesday. Several commissions — including ethics, elections, judicial discipline and public defenders — will present their budgets Thursday.
The budget committee will continue to meet three times a week for the rest of October, with one final meeting Nov. 6, to hear the rest of the state agencies’ proposed budgets.
The Department of Education will present its budget proposal Oct. 28. Lawmakers from both parties have expressed concerns in recent months about the increasing cost of the state’s school voucher program, created in 2023 and open to all students as of the 2025-26 school year. Sanders, who is running for reelection, has made the voucher program one of her highest priorities.
The Department of Human Services will present its budget Oct. 29 amid ongoing uncertainty about the future of Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion program. The federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services verbally declined to renew the program in July, and DHS requested a two-year grace period in August to keep Arkansans covered while the state chooses a new Medicaid model.
Looming federal cuts prompt concerns about food aid in Arkansas

DHS has not yet received a formal notification of the denial, nor has it received a response to the grace period request, agency spokesperson Gavin Lesnick said Tuesday.
Arkansas officials did not increase DHS’ budget for fiscal year 2026, raising concerns from advocates that the agency will not have the resources to handle the rising administrative cost of food stamps. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program is expected to cost DHS an extra $24 million within the next couple years thanks to a 2025 federal budget overhaul.
More than 330,000 Americans lost access to SNAP between May and June, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire Supreme Court denies death row inmate’s latest appeal
description: Seven years after repealing the death penalty, New Hampshire has one inmate on death row. On Tuesday, the state Supreme Court declined to intervene in his case, citing statutory authority. Michael Addison has been in prison for roughly 20 years for fatally shooting Manchester Police Officer Michael Briggs in 2006. In 2008, a jury sentenced […]
text:
The New Hampshire Supreme Court was asked to review the proportionality of Michael Addison's death sentence. (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)Seven years after repealing the death penalty, New Hampshire has one inmate on death row. On Tuesday, the state Supreme Court declined to intervene in his case, citing statutory authority.
Michael Addison has been in prison for roughly 20 years for fatally shooting Manchester Police Officer Michael Briggs in 2006. In 2008, a jury sentenced him to death. He was the last person to receive the death penalty before state lawmakers abolished it in 2019. However, the Legislature made the bill forward-looking, meaning that existing sentences like Addison’s could still be carried out.
Addison has spent the past decade and a half appealing his sentence with the American Civil Liberties Union’s recent support. Addison’s attorneys and the ACLU of New Hampshire argued that the state can’t execute him while it was forbidden by law from executing everyone else and that racial bias against Addison, who is Black, affected his sentence. The ACLU of New Hampshire compared him, in a 2025 “friend of the court” brief, to two other convicted murderers in New Hampshire — John Brooks in 2006 and Gordon Perry in 1998 — in which the courts found a stronger intent to kill but a jury sentenced the defendant to life in prison instead of death. They asked the court to review the proportionality of the case.
However, on Tuesday, the court declined to do so because it had already reviewed the proportionality of the case in 2015, at which point it determined that Addison’s sentence was “neither excessive nor disproportionate.” Justices argued that the state Legislature has authority over how death penalties are reviewed, and the Legislature did not give them the authority to review it again.
“If the legislature intended to provide successive comparative proportionality reviews for defendants convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death prior to the effective date of the act repealing the death penalty,” Justice Melissa Countway wrote in her opinion dismissing the appeal, “it could have included that in the legislation, but it did not.”
Gov. Kelly Ayotte, the former attorney general who prosecuted Addison’s case and has publicly called to revive the death penalty, celebrated the court’s decision.
“Michael Addison should face the death penalty for murdering Manchester Police Officer Michael Briggs in cold blood nearly 20 years ago,” Ayotte said in a statement. “Addison’s sentence was handed down fairly and in accordance with the law by a jury of his peers, and today’s ruling by the New Hampshire Supreme Court is an important step toward ensuring justice for Officer Briggs, the Briggs family, and the men and women of the Manchester Police Department.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC expanding student loan forgiveness for teachers in effort to keep them in the classroom
description: South Carolina is spending $10 million to help more teachers pay off or erase their student loans.
text:
Under a new program, South Carolina teachers who have federal or private student loan debt can apply to refinance as much as $27,500 worth of those loans for a fixed, 2% rate over 10 years, and in some cases, have that debt forgiven. (Stock photo bu Halfpoint Images via Getty)COLUMBIA — South Carolina is spending $10 million to help more teachers pay off or erase their student loans.
Legislators tucked the money in the latest state budget for the new program operated by South Carolina Student Loan Corp.
Under the program, teachers who have federal or private student loan debt can apply to refinance as much as $27,500 worth of those loans for a fixed, 2% rate over 10 years. In some cases, that debt can be forgiven.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ray Jones, chief product officer of SC Student Loan, estimates the program will reduce or eliminate debt for upwards of 360 working teachers in the state.
The nonprofit loan organization will split the state funds — $5 million to refinance at the lower interest rate and $5 million to wipe out loans for teachers who continue working in high-need school districts for five years.
“I believe public education is the foundation for the success of our state’s young people,” said Rep. Neal Collins. “This program is intended to provide financial support for teachers to keep them in the classroom. This is our way of showing them their service is important to the people, especially the children, of South Carolina.”
The Easley Republican sponsored the rule included in the state budget and supported the one-time funding for it. While the dollars apply only to the current fiscal year, he thinks legislators will likely keep the program in place indefinitely.
SC has a surplus in teacher loan repayments as more exit the field

“We’ve been investing in education, in my opinion, pretty heavily and I think it’s starting to show,” Collins told the SC Daily Gazette. “I’m encouraged about the direction of our state, as far as teachers are concerned. But, obviously, we have a long way to go as well.”
Retention versus recruitment
SC Student Loan, on behalf of the state, has operated the SC Teacher Loan program since 1984.
College students studying to be teachers can apply for the loan to cover their tuition. When they graduate, if they teach in what the state education agency deems a “critical” district or subject area for five years, they can apply to have it forgiven.
For the current school year, 45 of the state’s 74 public school districts qualify as critical, as do more than 30 subject areas.
The state designed that program as a recruitment tool to convince more South Carolina college students to pursue a degree and career in education.
This new program is different, aimed as an incentive to keep teachers in the classroom — those who, for whatever reason, did not take out loans through the legacy Teacher Loan program.
While the teacher shortage crisis has lessened, vacancies remain an issue. Districts started last school year with 706 empty teaching positions, according to the latest report from the Center for Educator Recruitment, Retention and Advancement.
“Our idea was those that didn’t get the Teacher Loan in the past or didn’t get the maximum still need an opportunity to have a low payment or have a forgiveness option,” Jones told the SC Daily Gazette. “What we’re hoping is to show some successful refinancing of mostly private educational debt that may have very high interest rates.”
These South Carolinians owed more than $120,000 in student loans. Now their debt is forgiven.

Some for-profit lenders charge interest rates of 12% to 16%, Jones added, and even federal loans come with rates of 8% or 9%.
“We believe if they refinance that debt into this 2% rate, that could be a huge cost savings for our teachers,” he said.
For example, someone with a $20,000 loan at a 10% interest rate is going to pay about $12,000 in interest over 10 years. Refinancing under this new program would take that down to $2,000 in interest and monthly loan payments would decrease by about $100.
“South Carolina’s teachers are doing some of the most important work in our state, and we want them to know we have their backs,” state education Superintendent Ellen Weaver said in a statement. “By helping educators keep more of their hard-earned money in their pockets, we’re investing in them and removing one more barrier to building a long and rewarding career serving South Carolina students.”
High demand
Jones is expecting high demand for the program. Applications began pouring in Monday, the first day it opened.
Patrick Kelly, a lobbyist for Palmetto State Teachers Association, agrees.
“I think it’s a fantastic use of state funds,” Kelly told the SC Daily Gazette. “This is a really important tool for educator retention in South Carolina.”
For starters, Kelly said, a surprising number of education majors go into college unaware of the Teacher Loan program and missed out on the opportunity to apply while working on their degree.
And when it comes to forgiveness of federal student loans, the program that wipes out any debt remaining after 10 years of payments for those working in public service careers “is not as robust as it once was,” Kelly said.
The U.S. Department of Education, in July, enacted changes to the program that is already facing major backlogs.
“So this is really a strong move by the state to backfill that,” Kelly said.
South Carolina also is one of the fastest growing states in the country. Educators who moved here from elsewhere and keep teaching may also apply to refinance any student loans they still have.
To fill teacher vacancies, SC could accept certificates from other states

And the number of teachers who get certified through alternative programs in the state rather than studying education in college is growing, Kelly said. These might be people with English or math degrees or who worked in a different field but later decided to pursue teaching careers.
The new loan refinancing or forgiveness would apply to any loans they took out to get their non-teaching degree.
Nearly half of all teachers — 47% — in the state entered through a traditional undergraduate degree, according to researchers at the University of South Carolina. Alternatively certified teachers and those licensed in other states make up about 30% of the workforce, a sizable share.
Those same teachers carry a significant amount of student loan debt. In a survey of its members, the Palmetto State Teachers Association found half have debt of $30,000 or more.
“In a profession like teaching, where the minimum starting wage in the state is $50,500, having that much debt is really a significant financial burden,” Kelly said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA Supreme Court candidates make their case as high-profile election nears
description: Less than a month remains until an election that will transform Washington’s state Supreme Court.  Two new justices will join the nine-member high court, and two new justices appointed by Gov. Bob Ferguson with no prior judicial experience face their first tests at the ballot box. The chief justice is also seeking another term.  It’s […]
text:
The Washington state Supreme Court building in Olympia. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)Less than a month remains until an election that will transform Washington’s state Supreme Court. 
Two new justices will join the nine-member high court, and two new justices appointed by Gov. Bob Ferguson with no prior judicial experience face their first tests at the ballot box. The chief justice is also seeking another term. 
It’s very rare to have a majority of the court up for election in one year. 
Much of the focus on the candidates is on how they’d decide cases, including on civil and criminal matters, especially as Washington’s new high-earners income tax is set to go before the court. But the justices also set the conversation on the direction of the court system. For example, the justices last year slashed caseload limits for public defenders, and will soon consider reforms to bail bond policy. 
Combined, justice candidates have raised well over $2 million for their campaigns, far more than in past election cycles when races drew far less competition and attention. 
The races serve as statewide proxy battles between conservatives and liberals, with four challengers endorsed by the state Republican Party against candidates favored by Democratic leaders. Formally, the races are nonpartisan.
In recent forums in Lacey and with the King County Bar Association, the candidates listed the most pressing challenges facing the judicial system, the role of artificial intelligence in the justice system and public perception of the court, among other topics. Judicial candidates are barred from discussing legal issues that could come before the court during the campaign.
Ballots will be mailed to voters by Oct. 16. Election Day is Nov. 3.
Position 1
Justice Colleen Melody has put a heavy focus in the campaign on the work the Supreme Court does outside of hearing oral arguments and issuing decisions on cases. Currently, those issues include language interpreter shortages, immigration arrests at courthouses and limited court system accessibility.
“We need to be talking with the judges and the court administrators on the ground in the different communities to understand what barriers they’re facing and to do kind of real elbow grease solutions to find solutions to those, so that we can have a court system that can and should be the envy of the nation,” Melody said.
Tax attorney Scott Edwards, who has support from the state Republican Party, wants to be an “independent voice” with a focus on the rule of law on the court. His priority to improve the court system is to “restore trust in the Supreme Court itself.”
“We have constitutional elections for Supreme Court, I believe, because of concern about appointed justices being likely to have the same philosophy and pursue the same policy objectives as the person that appointed them, and Supreme Court justices should be responsible to the people, not to the governor,” Edwards said.
Melody joined the court upon Ferguson’s appointment at the beginning of 2026, after the retirement of Justice Mary Yu. She defended Washington’s system of selecting justices.
“I have to stand immediately for my election right after being appointed, and you get an immediate say on whether you want me or not, and that’s a much more accountable system than what happens at the federal level, where once judges are appointed, they hold their position for life and they don’t stand for election ever again,” Melody said.
Edwards also takes issue with Melody thinking so much of a justice’s work is in overseeing the state’s judicial system, beyond the Supreme Court.
“My opponent believes that half of the job is being an advocate to the legislature and an advocate for other things,” Edwards said. “Her entire career was advocating for certain constituents.”
Melody joined the court after serving as the head of the civil rights division in the state attorney general’s office. She thinks Edwards would face a “pretty steep learning curve” going from tax attorney to Supreme Court justice. He has tried cases before the court, including an unsuccessful challenge to the state’s capital gains tax.
Melody has the support of many Democratic groups.
Position 3
Much attention is on how the justices feel about adhering to legal precedent, given a nearly century-old decision from the state Supreme Court ruling a progressive income tax unconstitutional. 
King County Superior Court Judge Jaime Hawk said “overturning precedent should be approached very cautiously and carefully, and has to meet those thresholds of incorrect and or wrongfully decided and harmful.” She pointed to decisions in recent years to overturn “harmful and incorrect” precedents in the wake of the racial justice movement.
Her election foe, Mason County Superior Court Judge David Stevens, pointed to the court’s Blake decision in 2021 striking down Washington’s drug criminalization law as a case where overturning precedent was done poorly, even if he agrees that state statute may not have been constitutional.
 

David Stevens, 2026 candidate for Washington state Supreme Court, speaks at a forum in Lacey. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)
 

Stevens shared Edwards’ concern about appointed justices. Noting proposed changes to the bail system and juvenile cases, Stevens said he believes the current justices are “fundamentally changing the criminal justice system in Washington state, and I think this is because they’re ideologically driven.”
Hawk called for upping juror pay. Most Washington jurors are paid $10 per day. This hasn’t changed since 1959, creating a barrier to a true jury of one’s peers in local courts, she said. 
 Position 4
State appeals court Judge Ian Birk found himself in hot water recently for calling his opponent, King County Superior Court Judge Sean O’Donnell, a closet Republican. This led to a letter from dozens of judges calling out Birk for his partisan comments. O’Donnell says he has support from both sides of the political spectrum.

Sean O’Donnell, 2026 candidate for Washington state Supreme Court. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)

Despite the controversy, Birk said he sees the work of a jurist as “an inherently non-political thing.”
O’Donnell thinks voters have three reasons to vote for him: “My experience, my impartiality, and my ability to have a vision and work with others to get stuff done.” 
More than other candidates, O’Donnell has played up the importance of the Supreme Court setting rules for the use of generative artificial intelligence for judges and lawyers. He cited a spike in litigants filing court briefs using this technology. He thinks its use should be limited.
Birk agrees AI will be a major topic of conservation for years in the legal field.
“On the other hand, we’re not close to having it generate legal work product yet because it doesn’t understand the difference between stringing together words likely to come after the ones that have already been put down versus making a cogent, coherent argument that’s rooted in law and and what the law is trying to accomplish,” he said. 

Ian Birk, 2026 candidate for Washington state Supreme Court. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)
 
O’Donnell said the court’s decision to slash public defender caseloads was undertaken “without a plan how to make it work, and we’re seeing the consequences of that now across the state.” Birk said he’d like to see the Supreme Court slow down its rulemaking process, and said he’d work with the Legislature as a justice to smooth the rollout of those new caseload standards.
Birk and O’Donnell will meet for a debate Friday morning streamed by TVW. 
The winner of this campaign will replace retiring Justice Charles Johnson.
Position 5
Justice Theo Angelis is running to retain his seat on the court for the first time. Ferguson appointed Angelis to the court this year after Justice Barbara Madsen’s retirement.
His opponent, Dave Larson, is a retired Federal Way Municipal Court judge.
Larson, like Stevens and Edwards, wants to reform the way new judges are selected. He is calling for a bipartisan Judicial Elections Commission to bring agreed-upon candidates for the governor to consider for appointment. He has support from the state Republican Party, and nearly won a campaign to join the court two years ago.
Angelis takes issue with the notion that you can tell how a justice will rule on a given issue based on who appointed them. He promised to be “an independent thinker.”

Dave Larson, 2026 candidate for Washington state Supreme Court. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)

“But the reality is this: all of us have individual experiences and biases that color our thinking of issues that come before us,” he said. “If we identify the potential biases that we have, we can do a good job in counteracting them. So for every case that comes before our court, I actually make a physical list of potential biases.”
Angelis said he’s already had to rule in ways he thought were incorrect in his short time on the court, “but that’s what the law requires.”
Angelis, like Hawk, called for updating pay for jurors.
Position 7
Chief Justice Debra Stephens, who has been on the court since 2008, takes issue with critics who believe judges are motivated by ideology.
“I think some of the people who say it just comes down to ideology listen to what other people think, and they don’t necessarily read what the courts have written,” Stephens said. “In some ways, to be a judge with integrity, you have to just let the chips fall where they may in terms of that perception, and do the careful, detailed work of walking through precedent, which is what I try to do every day in writing difficult decisions.”

Todd Bloom is challenging Debra Stephens, chief justice of the Washington state Supreme Court, in the November 2026 election. candidate for Washington state Supreme Court. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)

Todd Bloom, an attorney and veteran, thinks he and his opponent would reach their decisions differently. 
“‘What does that constitution actually say, and what do the court cases actually say?’ Bloom said of his approach. “Instead of trying to figure out what the values are and then discern how I’m going to write the result either to support my interpretation of the values or some other policy resolve.”
Bloom has the backing of the state GOP, while Stephens has the support of all of her colleagues on the court.

title: State, plaintiffs agree to settle lawsuit over NH in-home care program after five-year court battle
description: The New Hampshire Department and Health and Human Services, facing a class-action lawsuit over its in-home care program for older adults and people with physical disabilities, agreed to a settlement with plaintiffs Monday. A group of nonprofits — including the AARP Foundation, the Disability Rights Center-NH and New Hampshire Legal Assistance, as well as the[...]
text:
The U.S. District Court, District of New Hampshire in Concord. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)The New Hampshire Department and Health and Human Services, facing a class-action lawsuit over its in-home care program for older adults and people with physical disabilities, agreed to a settlement with plaintiffs Monday.
A group of nonprofits — including the AARP Foundation, the Disability Rights Center-NH and New Hampshire Legal Assistance, as well as the law firm Nixon Peabody — sued the state in 2021 in federal court over the lackluster state of its Choices for Independence program.
Choices for Independence seeks to allow the elderly and those with disabilities to stay in their homes instead of being placed in nursing facilities. To do this, the program provides funding to hire in-home care aides. Evidence presented in court showed placement in a facility is three times more expensive for the state, and most participants say they’d rather remain in their own homes. However, participants struggle to actually receive the care because of staffing shortages and, the plaintiffs argued, underfunding by the state.
The lawsuit, which became a class-action suit in 2023, alleged that by underfunding the program, the state is violating participants’ legal rights to remain in their communities by unnecessarily forcing them into nursing homes. It was set to go to trial next month.
However, after half a decade of legal fighting, the two sides have come to an agreement. If U.S. District Court Judge Paul Barbadoro approves the settlement, the trial won’t happen. Instead, the state and the plaintiffs have agreed to a deal in which DHHS will implement a series of remedies for the program. In agreeing to the deal, DHHS did not admit to any wrongdoing, law violations or liability.
“I think it’s a very hopeful moment that we’re in,” Kelly Bagby, an attorney with the AARP Foundation and lead counsel for the plaintiffs, said. “And I do think that it will require vigilance by the plaintiffs’ lawyers to continue to monitor. It will require DHHS to really embrace the settlement. But I think finally the CFI participants will have a voice in their own care, and they’ll have that voice through the grievance system, through the request for specialized rates. If they can’t get a service provider, they’ll have a voice in being able to tell DHHS whether they think they’re doing a good job or not. And I think that has also not existed before.”
That deal would require DHHS to hire a third-party consultant to analyze the network of care aides to determine whether it meets the needs of the participants. Specifically, the analysis would determine the level of service the state approved for participants and how much they actually received, among other things. DHHS has agreed to complete this analysis within 180 days of the settlement being finalized and again annually thereafter.
DHHS has also agreed to ensure that every participant has a contingency plan in place should they not receive their approved services. Additionally, it agreed to identify any participants who have received less than 50% of their services each month and require the case management agency (the agency managing the care) to execute the contingency plan.
Care aide salaries are determined in part by DHHS reimbursement rates. People in the program have consistently reported that caregiver pay is so low it makes hiring close to impossible. DHHS has agreed to perform an analysis on its reimbursement rates and methodologies for the program. It also agreed to ask state lawmakers for biennial increases to match inflation.
In the past, DHHS has sometimes offered specialized rates to care aides if it determined that it was unable to hire anyone due to low pay. The plaintiffs argued DHHS offered these specialized rates infrequently. Under this agreement, DHHS “shall amend its Specialized Rates policy to facilitate the expeditious use of Specialized Rates to address CFI Service Gaps.”
“That system has been very limited,” Bagby said. “I think maybe roughly 200 people ever got a specialized rate.”
DHHS has also agreed to create an online portal and directory of aides. This directory will include names, contact information, whether the aide is accepting new clients, the counties the aide serves and more. The directory would be available through an online portal.
Finally, DHHS agreed to expand its existing grievance system, where participants can file complaints about the program, to include complaints about missed services.
Every six months, DHHS would be required under this agreement to create a report outlining its compliance with the agreement. Asked if she’s concerned the reforms won’t be enough to fix the program, Bagby said she and her colleagues will be watching the state’s moves, “and you know that’s our job, and we will be very passionately pursuing it.” She also said the plaintiffs’ attorneys plan to hold virtual sessions where participants can learn about the settlement process in November.
“Older adults and people with disabilities deserve access to the services they need to live safely and independently in their homes and communities,” Attorney General John Formella, who led the agency that fought the lawsuit for the past five years, said in a statement. “This settlement strengthens accountability and oversight of the Choices for Independence program and provides a framework to address service gaps. The Department of Justice will continue working with DHHS and our partners to support implementation.”
Michael Garrity, deputy chief of staff for communications and external affairs at the Department of Justice, declined to make anyone available for an interview with the Bulletin, saying in an email the department had nothing further to add.
“I think it’s a happy day for CFI participants,” Bagby said. “I think we’re at a hopeful point, and again, reforms take time, but I feel like we’re at the beginning of those reforms now.”

name: WyoFile
title: Tweak to Endangered Species Act could allow widespread development
description:
Trump officials tout “‘harm”’ change to unleash energy agenda, as critics warn it could unravel 50 years of ecological recovery
The post Tweak to Endangered Species Act could allow widespread development appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Every ecosystem has a “keystone” species whose presence or absence affects everything else in the landscape. The legal system works in a similar way.
A series of recent U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service changes aimed at the Endangered Species Act appear to consider the 1973 law as the keystone to unleashing resource development, according to both federal agency leaders and environmental activists challenging the Trump administration policies in court. In particular, they warn that a rule changing the definition of a single word in the ESA could effectively gut it.
“They’re coming for the Endangered Species Act from multiple directions,” said Earthjustice attorney Tim Preso, who is representing a coalition of environmental groups challenging the rule change. “This is about pulling away the safety net from the most imperiled wildlife in service of their deregulatory agenda.”
Ever since its passage, the ESA has created tension between the needs of imperiled animals and plants and the desires of humans seeking to use the same landscape. The law protects those species from extinction mainly by prohibiting their “take,” a legal term meaning to put under human control. The word “take” was defined as “harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture or collect.” Within that list, the word “harm” meant “significant habitat modification or degradation where it actually kills or injures wildlife.”
A Federal Register notice that took effect on Sept. 14 rescinded the ESA’s definition of “harm” in the list of words defining “take,” something the Trump administration had sought since the early 2025. It redefined “take” to mean “only an affirmative act that is intentionally and purposefully directed at a particular animal.” Finally, it advised that “only action directed at living animals constitutes a ‘take,’ so destroying [essential] habitat … would not violate the Act,” adding “modification of unoccupied habitat is never a take, however certain its eventual effect on the species.” 
The word “take” forms the heart of the ESA’s protective power, according to an analysis by University of Montana law professor and ESA expert Sandra Zellmer.
“Habitat modification is the primary reason for [ESA] listing,” Zellmer wrote in her 2026 American Bar Association journal paper. “If modifying habitat is no longer a ‘take,’ the ESA itself would be rendered incapable of satisfying Congress’ goal: ‘to halt and reverse the trend toward species extinction, whatever the cost.’” 
While the “take” rule has earned lots of attention in recent days, it’s far from the only ESA change in the works. Preso listed several more federal actions aimed at dismantling ESA authority. 
For example, he noted FWS also plans to revoke what’s known as the “blanket rule” which gives ESA-listed threatened species the same level of protection as endangered species while more tailored recovery plans are under development. And the Forest Service’s recent intention to repeal the Roadless Rule could undermine ESA protections for listed grizzly bears, because federal grizzly recovery plans depend on the bears having roadless habitat for security. 
Trump executive orders issued in 2025 also targeted the ESA as an impediment to energy development. Many of those concerns have been wrapped into a congressional bill for widespread permitting reform of energy and infrastructure projects, which is nearing final passage this fall. In an email, Western Environmental Law Center spokesman Erik Schlenker-Goodrich told Mountain Journal in an email the bill would “prove to be the largest rollback of environmental and public health protections in U.S. history, weakening the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, National Environmental Policy Act, and more.”
Endangered species fall under the oversight of multiple agencies within the departments of Interior and Commerce. Those in turn impose ESA regulations on other federal, state and private stakeholders, including the U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management, state wildlife agencies, and ranchers, farmers, miners and loggers.
Asked for comment on the September imposition of the rule, an Interior press official only provided a July 10 press release from Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stating the move terminates an outdated regulation that caused years of federal overreach.
“For years, federal agencies abused the ESA to obstruct lawful land use and burden American families and businesses,” Burgum said in the release. “That approach turned routine activity into a regulatory trap, drove up costs that impacted people’s lives, and expanded federal authority beyond what Congress intended. This action restores common sense, respects private property, provides much-needed certainty for landowners and follows the statute Congress actually passed.”
U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum speaks in June 2025 at the Western Governors’ Association conference in Santa Fe, New Mexico. (Ellen Jaskol)
Noah Greenwald of the Center for Biological Diversity, which Earthjustice is representing against the federal government, claimed the Fish and Wildlife Service is throwing out the landmark environmental legislation.
“It’s a radical departure from how the ESA has been interpreted and implemented for more than 50 years,” Greenwald said. “I would say it’s a ‘scorched earth, we don’t care anymore’ policy.”
Greenwald added that while the change was likely to spend years in court, actual damage to ESA-protected species could happen much faster. Animals that depend on pristine habitat, such as bull trout or spotted owls, could disappear as logging or mining projects win approval without ESA consultations under the new rules, he said.
Few organizations have commented openly in support of the change, or have heralded its passage. One, the Association of General Contractors of America, posted its argument favoring the rescission on its website, stating the “prospect of take (including incidental take) of a species or destruction of habitat is a significant risk and concern for construction contractors … AGC appreciates the administration’s efforts to reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens — especially for the recognition that take or harm implies an intention or affirmative act.”
President Richard Nixon signed the Endangered Species Act in 1973, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service published its first definition of the word “harm” in 1981, declaring it meant “significant habitat modification or degradation where it actually kills or injures wildlife by significantly impairing essential behavioral patterns, including breeding, feeding or sheltering.” The Supreme Court upheld that definition in a 1995 case, Babbitt v. Sweet Home.
On the losing side of that decision, Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia’s dissenting opinion essentially mashed all the “take” nesting dolls together under a legal principle known as “noscitur a sociis,” meaning “a word is known by the company it keeps.” The other definitions of “take” all referred to direct injury to a specific animal, in Scalia’s reasoning. “Harm” improperly added indirect injuries to the definition, which allowed federal agencies to create unfair regulations about land use.
On the winning side, six justices agreed that the word “harm” in endangered species management specifically referred to habitat modification. The majority ruling also directly rejected Scalia’s “noscitur a sociis” argument, noting that if all the words meant the same thing, there was no point in using so many different ones.
That opinion held until a 2024 Supreme Court case opened the door for the rule change, according to an Ohio State University analysis. Loper Bright v. Raimondo overturned the Sweet Home decision by getting rid of another Supreme Court precedent known as “Chevron deference.” For decades, Chevron deference required judges to accept an agency’s opinion or policy if the congressional law was ambiguous or the agency’s response was reasonable. The majority in Loper Bright held instead that judges should make those determinations based on who made the best argument in court. The Trump administration took that a step further.
“According to the agencies, [Loper Bright] left open the possibility that the executive branch could … depart from regulations that do not match the single, best meaning of the statute,” the OSU analysis stated. “This, coupled with Scalia’s dissent in Sweet Home, is the agencies’ basis for rescinding the definition of “harm.”
“The Services are persuaded instead by Justice Scalia’s analysis as to what the correct construction of the statutory text is,” FWS stated in its Federal Register publication. “The Court left open the possibility that the executive branch could itself depart from regulations that do not match the single, best meaning of the statute — so long as the new regulations reflect that best meaning.”
In the Sept. 14 legal guidance memos, Interior and Commerce officials explained the new rule clarifies that unintentional “take” was no longer a concern of the ESA. In an example, the memo said someone draining a pond to kill a turtle would be breaking the law if the person deliberately wanted to “take” the turtle. “When that purpose is absent, there is no take, however serious the resulting injury may be. A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel’s course was not set against the whale.”
Preso called that “180 degrees opposite” of what the ESA has meant since 1973. “And not only are they picking their own interpretation,” he told Mountain Journal, “they’re picking the one rejected by a majority of the Supreme Court when it was before the Supreme Court. Everything’s upside-down.”
The rule change received about 358,000 public comments, according to its Federal Register tally. FWS declined requests to hold public hearings and extend the 30-day review period on the proposal. 
The CBD lawsuit is one of at least seven filed since the Trump administration changed the definition of the word “take” in its interpretation of how the federal government oversees the habitat used by endangered and threatened animals and plants. Other challengers include two Native American tribes, a coalition of 21 states, and numerous environmental organizations. Most suits were filed in July, shortly after the rule change was finalized in the Federal Register. The federal government has until early October to respond.

title: DeSantis boasts about Medicaid fraud crackdown efforts
description: Gov. Ron DeSantis appeared in West Palm Beach Tuesday to announce the fruits of the state’s Medicaid fraud and abuse crackdown efforts, including more than 150 referrals to the state’s attorney general’s Medicaid fraud unit to investigate and potentially prosecute. DeSantis said the state also has restricted or suspended payments to more than 260 providers [[...]
text:
Applied Behavior Analysis encourages positive behavior and discourages negative behavior for autism and other special-needs patients. 
(Photo by Jack Forrest/ Indiana Capital Chronicle)Gov. Ron DeSantis appeared in West Palm Beach Tuesday to announce the fruits of the state’s Medicaid fraud and abuse crackdown efforts, including more than 150 referrals to the state’s attorney general’s Medicaid fraud unit to investigate and potentially prosecute.
DeSantis said the state also has restricted or suspended payments to more than 260 providers suspected of Medicaid fraud and has, since the beginning of the year, terminated 220 providers from the state’s program. 
“These actions are focused on bad actors who exploit the program, not legitimate providers delivering necessary care to Floridians,” DeSantis said. He added that the data underscore “exactly why the heightened oversight is essential.”
He said the referrals and suspensions were the first “salvo” and promised more to come.
SentiLink is assisting the state with its fraud and abuse efforts, DeSantis announced in June, and is conducting a “large-scale identity intelligence analysis covering millions of individuals and entities enrolled in the Florida Medicaid program.” 
The goal of the contract, according to the press release announcing the agreement between the state and the company, is “to detect sophisticated fraud schemes — not just individual bad actors — including organized networks operating through concealed ownerships, fictitious entities, and compromised credentials.”
The DeSantis administration announced enhanced Medicaid fraud and abuse efforts after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services sent a letter to Florida ( as well as California, Maine, and New York) seeking information about Medicaid integrity and oversight — and after CMS Director Mehmet Oz said on social media that “Florida has been a hotspot for health care fraud for years.”
The Florida Agency for Health Care Administration has conducted more than 400 onsite provider visits with the focus on those that provide people access to durable medical equipment, adult day care, and applied behavioral analysis, a therapy provided to children with autism and people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. 
“We’re knocking on more doors, conducting site visits. We’re not leaving if the provider does not produce the records requested,” AHCA Secretary Shevaun Harris said. “We’re not accepting, ‘I didn’t know the requirements,’ as an answer.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Harris said the agency has required Medicaid providers to verify their credentials and identities as part of its beefed-up fraud efforts.
 She acknowledged it can be bothersome but insisted it’s necessary.
“These fraudsters have sophisticated schemes. It’s forcing us to be nimble and agile and to use every tool at our disposal to combat this issue,” she said.
Structured interventions
ABA represents structured interventions to decrease maladaptive behaviors and reinforce appropriate ones. It is common in treatment of children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder and used for people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), traumatic brain injuries, and intellectual and developmental disabilities. 
Shena Grantham, Florida’s deputy secretary for Medicaid policy and quality, said in August that about 60,000 low-income children in Florida receive ABA, although she didn’t cite the year.
The protocol has been a focus of the state’s fraud and abuse efforts for years, and past efforts to better control costs and detect fraud included pilot programs and a moratorium on ABA provider enrollments. But costs kept increasing.
Then Florida switched its ABA delivery model to require managed care plans to cover services for children. Previously, patients, once authorized, saw the Medicaid ABA provider of their choice and the state paid for the services.
Since 2025, the care must be provided by the state-contracted plans and the ABA providers who want to continue working with their clients are having to negotiate contracts in their regions.
Before the switch to managed care, economists predicted ABA services would reach $3.86 billion in state FY 26-27, the governor said.
ABA expenditures are now projected to come in at $2.88 billion, he continued.
Why does Florida spend so much money on treatment for children with autism and special needs?

Some ABA providers have been dropped from the managed care networks and others have chosen to stop treating Medicaid clients.
Families and providers have been complaining about interruptions in ABA services since the transition to managed care.
When asked about difficulties parents have been reporting in getting care for their children since then, DeSantis was stern.
“You know, to the extent that those services get interrupted, that’s not AHCA’s fault. That’s the providers’ fault for what they’re doing and putting those families in that situation,” DeSantis said. “And, unfortunately, you know, we’ve seen that.”
Harris said state contracted managed care plans “have staff on deck who are providing care coordination services, reaching out to these families, and helping them pick a new provider so there are no gaps or interruption in services.” Parents struggling to secure services for their children can contact AHCA.
“We will help help them ourselves or connect them with with their managed care plan,” she said.
The Florida Legislature this spring created a 10-member task force and directed it to review the delivery model “to  improve care experience and service continuity for enrollees and families receiving ABA services, while safeguarding long term program sustainability.”
The panel has met four times and is expected to hold an additional two meetings before finalizing its recommendations.

title: UVM Medical Center unions reach tentative agreement in contract negotiations
description:
Union members now have until Sunday to vote on ratifying the contract.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM Medical Center unions reach tentative agreement in contract negotiations.
text:
Union doctors and staff workers at the University of Vermont Medical Center, along with their supporters, during a rally in Burlington in June 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Both the support staff and technical professional unions at the University of Vermont Medical Center have reached tentative, two-year contract agreements with their employer, both the hospital and union representatives confirmed Tuesday. 
The agreement comes just days after both unions voted to give their bargaining teams the OK to call for a strike. The tentative agreement now goes to a vote for union members on whether to ratify the contracts. Voting is set to open on Wednesday and run through Sunday, according to union representatives. 
“I’m grateful to our union partners for their collaboration and commitment to working with us, remaining at the bargaining table and reaching an agreement that recognizes the important contributions of our employees and supports our ability to care for our region for many years to come,” Dr. Steven Leffler, the president and CEO of UVM Medical Center and its parent company, wrote in a statement. 
“Months of thoughtful work went into reaching this agreement and we look forward to building on the productive discussions that focus on supporting our people, providing high-quality care for our patients and our shared commitment to addressing the affordability challenges facing all Vermonters,” he said. 
UVM Medical Center is facing steep losses in revenue and striving to cut its expenses. The network has cut more than 300 positions, in two rounds of layoffs in June and September, as part of its effort to reduce expenses. Those combined cuts included managerial staff and union members alike, all across the UVM Health system. More staff cuts are inevitable, hospital executives said in September.
The two unions have been jointly negotiating new contracts since April. Together, the support staff and technical professionals unions represent more than 3,000 employees at the Burlington medical center. The support staff union includes workers such as licensed nursing assistants and schedulers, while the technical professionals’ union includes roles such as lab and sterilization technicians.
Negotiations have centered around issues of staffing levels, with the unions pushing the hospital management for more say in how many employees per floor constitutes a safe number. 
The joint-bargaining also pushed for a series of “common good” proposals, including a request for the hospital to cooperate with state efforts for universal healthcare and for the hospital to source dairy products through Migrant Justice’s Milk with Dignity program. 
Representatives from both the union and the hospital declined to offer more details on what is included in this tentative contract agreement until after the union vote.

title: Top Democratic US Senate PAC commits to 9 states, eyes more Republican targets
text:
A leading Democratic campaign committee is projecting confidence in U.S. Senate toss-up races four weeks before Election Day, though it has yet to commit resources to the reddest states that have recently entered the Senate map.Senate Majority PAC, which is run by allies of Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, has bought ad time, or has commitments to do so, in nine states, Lauren French, the group’s chief spokesperson told reporters Tuesday. Those states — Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas — show Democrats are competing this cycle in typically Republican places. Elections analysts generally say those states are toss-ups or lean Democratic.

 






(Photo by Getty images)

The Democratic super PAC’s slate, though, is not as expansive as some of the latest public polls and forecaster ratings show could be in play.The group is “watching really closely” the races in GOP strongholds of Florida, South Carolina, Mississippi and Kansas, French said. At least one of those states, Kansas, could be in play for the first time in decades, according to elections forecaster The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, which moved it into the toss-up category Tuesday.“Broadly, we are very pleased with the state of the race right now,” French said. “We are invested in nine battleground states and are looking very closely at some of the expansion states that are coming (into) play as we get four weeks from the election and the environment continues to be increasingly rough for Republicans.”An expanded Senate map is available to Democrats because of President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, especially tied to the Iran war and related high gas prices, French said. Trump’s approval rating is lower than his disapproval rating “in every battleground state,” she added.North Carolina movesOpportunities for Republicans appear to be shrinking, with North Carolina moving further toward Democrats. Cook shifted the race from lean Democrat to likely Democrat on Tuesday, after the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican super PAC, said last week it was freezing future spending in the state.French said the Senate Majority PAC also canceled its television and digital spending this week in the race for the seat left open by retiring Republican Thom Tillis. The group has not made decisions on spending in the Tar Heel State beyond this week, she said.Republicans hold cash edgeWhile the national political environment favors Democrats, the GOP and its fellow campaign groups maintain a massive cash advantage against Democrats.Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., held more than $400 million at the end of August, according to records filed with the Federal Election Commission. Senate Majority PAC showed around $57 million on hand in the same report.Fundraising numbers for official party committees also significantly favor Republicans. The Republican National Committee and the party’s campaign groups supporting House and Senate candidates outraised their Democratic counterparts by about $100 million through Aug. 31, according to an analysis by nonpartisan elections analyst Ballopedia. Republicans have largely aimed to portray Democrats as too far to the left to capably manage Congress.“Voters have a clear choice this November between Republicans who will fight for them and radical, socialist Democrats who would serve as rubber stamps for Chuck Schumer’s Washington machine,” Bernadette Breslin, a spokeswoman for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, said in a statement.Rare pickup opportunitiesStill, the Senate Majority PAC’s bullish sentiment broadly matches expert opinion, as forecasters continue to see a strong case for Democrats to pick up Senate seats. Republicans now control the Senate with 53 seats.The elections handicapper Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved two Senate races in Democrats’ direction Tuesday. The group labeled Alaska as leaning toward Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola in her challenge to incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan, and shifted U.S. Sen. Darline Graham’s reelection race in South Carolina from safe Republican to likely Republican.Overall, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, which operates at the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics, rates 49 seats, including those of incumbents not on the ballot this year, as at least leaning toward the Democrat, with four seen as toss-ups. Democrats, who now hold 47 seats, would need to net 51 seats to win a majority because Vice President JD Vance casts tie-breaking votes.A flip in control of the chamber would significantly slow Trump’s nominees to the federal bench and executive branch posts.

title: No major gains projected for count of women in Congress after midterms
text: WASHINGTON — The number of women in the U.S. Senate is unlikely to increase and may decline following the November midterm elections, though there are still opportunities for candidates to make history in the upper chamber.Kelly Dittmar, director of research at the Center for American Women and Politics, said on a call with reporters Tuesday that Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and Mary Peltola in Alaska, both Democrats, would become the first Native American women in the Senate if they’re elected. “And if Juliana Stratton wins in Illinois, a record three Black women will serve concurrently in the U.S. Senate for the first time in U.S. history,” Dittmar said. “Only five Black women have ever served in the U.S. Senate. So the three women who would be serving in the 120th Senate would represent 50%, or half, of all Black women who've ever served.”The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the Illinois race as solidly Democratic, the Minnesota election as likely Democratic and Alaska as a toss-up.When it comes to overall representation, voters would need to elect six new women to replace outgoing female senators and keep the number of women in that chamber level during the next Congress, which is set to begin in January. “At present, four women non-incumbents are favored to win in November, and two more non-incumbent women are in competitive contests,” Dittmar said. “In addition, one incumbent woman senator, Susan Collins in Maine, is currently deemed as vulnerable in her bid for re-election.”That means there would need to be some unexpected victories for women Senate candidates in order to actually increase representation in that chamber, likely leaving the percentage of women senators flat or in decline. Any path possible in HouseThe House of Representatives, where 125 of the 435 seats are held by women, is in a somewhat different position.There will be at least 271 women on the ballot for House seats, giving voters the opportunity to surpass the previous record of 127 women in that chamber at one time.  “Net gains, loss, or stasis all remain possible outcomes for women's U.S. House representation from 2026 to 2027,” Dittmar said. “And these are all possible outcomes as well when you look by party for Democratic women or Republican women specifically.”Democratic women hold a record of 95 seats, while Republican women have previously maxed out their representation at 34.No parity in either partyCAWP, part of the Eagleton Institute of Politics at New Jersey’s Rutgers University, aims to be a “leading source” of research and data on women in politics.Chelsea Hill, the group’s director of data, said there were a record 590 women running for a seat in Congress at the start of this year’s campaign cycle, though that number decreased as voters decided which candidates they wanted in this fall’s general election. “It's important to note, even with these candidacy records, women continue to be significantly underrepresented as a percentage of all U.S. House and U.S. Senate candidates,” Hill said. And while Democratic women are represented in higher numbers in their party than Republican women, neither has reached gender parity, she said. In total there are 198 Democratic and 73 Republican women candidates on ballots this fall, which Hill said is an increase from the last election cycle but “short of the record high of 298 women nominees for the U.S. House set in 2020.”“When broken down by race and ethnicity, only Latinas reached new highs for U.S. House candidacies and nominations this year,” she said. “On the Senate side, the number of Native American, Alaska Native, or Native Hawaiian women nominees for the U.S. Senate, three, is an historic high,” Hill added. “And the number of Black, four, and Latina, two, Senate nominees match existing records. Among women candidates for U.S. Senate, only white women have reached a new high of 45.”

name: VTDigger
title: Proposal 4’s language is flawed
description:
The Legislature’s own constitutional law expert has raised concerns about the amendment’s language.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Proposal 4’s language is flawed.
text:
Dear Editor,
Judy Olinick’s recent letter to VTDigger in response to Renee McGuinness’ commentary on Proposal 4, the so-called equality of rights amendment, contains misleading information.
First, the Vermont Constitution, Chapter II, Section 72, dictates that legislators must put a proposed amendment before voters once both chambers approve it in two successive sessions; their vote is not necessarily an indication of their support of the proposal itself. This is a critical procedural point that is easily misunderstood and is a valid reason to have in-depth public discussion and analysis of the potential consequences of these constitutional amendments.
Second, the negative consequences of Proposal 4’s passage are real. McGuinness pointed to the Senate and House Judiciary committees’ own expert witness, Peter Teachout, a Vermont Law and Graduate School professor whose field is state and federal constitutional law, who said he would vote against Proposal 4 because the language is “flawed” and the purpose section is “ambiguous.” Further, on May 1, 2024, as the House Judiciary Committee members discussed how courts would interpret the language of the proposal, Teachout said it would be up to the Vermont Supreme Court to determine the intent of the language, and joked, “It makes lawyers rich.” 

READ MORE

The House Judiciary Committee, the Senate and the House all knew they would be putting an amendment with flawed language before the voters, yet nearly all members voted in favor of putting Proposal 4 forward anyway. This is not good governance.
Robert FireovidSouth Hero, Vt.
