name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania’s public defense crisis is a constitutional crisis
description: The constitutional right to counsel is one of the cornerstones of American democracy. But a constitutional right without adequate funding is merely a promise on paper.
text:
A judge's gavel in a courtroom. ((Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)The constitutional right to counsel is one of the cornerstones of American democracy. But a constitutional right without adequate funding is merely a promise on paper. 
After years of chronic underfunding, the Defender Association of Philadelphia has been forced to make painful staffing reductions and reduce services that thousands of Pennsylvanians rely upon every year. 
The recent service reductions in Philadelphia should serve as a warning to the commonwealth: if the largest public defender office in Pennsylvania is reducing staffing to critical court programs — despite years of operational improvements, grant funding, and careful financial stewardship — the problem is structural underinvestment. 
These cuts are the predictable consequence of a system that has failed to invest in one of its most basic constitutional obligations. 
This is not simply Philadelphia’s problem. 
It is Pennsylvania’s.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While public attention mainly focuses on police, prosecutors, and prisons, public defenders are equally essential to a functioning justice system. An effective public defense system strengthens public safety. 
Defenders help identify people who need treatment rather than incarceration, reduce unnecessary pretrial detention, negotiate resolutions that hold people accountable while promoting rehabilitation, and ensure court proceedings move efficiently. 
Every part of the justice system functions better when public defenders have the resources to do their jobs well.
Pennsylvania remains an outlier nationally when it comes to funding public defense. For decades, it was one of the only states that did not provide recurring indigent defense funding, forcing counties to shoulder nearly the entire cost of this constitutional mandate. 
Although the commonwealth has finally begun investing in public defense, the current statewide appropriation of just $7.5 million is nowhere near enough to meet the need.
While local governments in New York and New Jersey still carry significant fiscal responsibilities for public defense, they still invest more than Pennsylvania. Neighboring states like  Delaware, Maryland and Massachusetts assume primary responsibility for funding statewide public defense systems. 
These states invest tens or hundreds of millions of dollars annually to ensure constitutional representation, regardless of where someone lives. 
Pennsylvania’s fractional investment creates a patchwork system, where justice depends largely on local resources instead of constitutional guarantees. In our Commonwealth, the quality of representation — and ultimately, access to justice — can vary dramatically depending on zip code.
A hallway in the Schuylkill County Courthouse in Pottsville on March 12, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
That is not what the Constitution promises.
Pennsylvania has already acknowledged that indigent defense is a statewide responsibility by appropriating state funds for the first time. 
Gov. Josh Shapiro and the General Assembly should move the state toward a funding model that reflects making an investment in public defense a priority. 
The commonwealth should move toward a funding model that reflects the true cost of providing effective representation in all 67 counties — not one that leaves local governments to shoulder nearly the entire burden.
Public defense is not a discretionary government program. It is a constitutional mandate. 
We would never expect police departments, prosecutors’ offices, or the courts to fulfill their responsibilities without adequate funding. We should not expect public defenders to do so either.
The Defender Association of Philadelphia’s decision to reduce some services is more than a local budget story. It is a warning that Pennsylvania’s constitutional promise is becoming increasingly difficult to keep. 
The question is not whether we can afford to invest in public defense. The question is whether we can afford not to.
A justice system is measured not only by how it prosecutes crime, but by how faithfully it protects the rights guaranteed to every person. 
Pennsylvania has an opportunity to demonstrate that those rights are more than words on paper.
 
Keisha Hudson is the Chief Defender at the Defender Association of Philadelphia, which represents about 75% of the youth and adults charged with crimes in the city. She has more than 20 years of experience providing legal counsel to Pennsylvania’s most economically vulnerable citizens.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A self-defense instructor’s thoughts on the Cornell sexual assault case
description:
I teach sexual assault prevention. And I'm going to tell you something most instructors won't say out loud. 
There is no technique for this.
text:
I’ve been teaching self-defense for 25 years. I teach people to strike, to escape, to fight when they have to. I teach sexual assault prevention. And I’m going to tell you something most instructors won’t say out loud.
There is no technique for this.
Look at what is unfolding at Cornell right now.
A former Cornell student says that in 2024 she was pressured to drink and take ketamine at the Chi Phi fraternity house until she could no longer function. Then, according to her lawsuit, seven men raped her over a period of hours. One of them allegedly advertised her in a fraternity group chat and invited his brothers to join in.
No one was arrested. No one was charged.
The only reason this story is in front of you now is that she filed a civil lawsuit this month. The public saw it. The public got angry. And only then did the district attorney reopen the case and announce he would take it to a grand jury.
Read that again. The system moved because of public outrage. Not because of what happened to her.
Cornell says it ran a months-long Title IX process. Her attorney says two of the seven were expelled. The rest got suspensions, workshops, and written assignments. The lawsuit alleges they were allowed to write essays to soften their punishment. Cornell denies that. But even by Cornell’s own account, most of the seven men accused of a gang rape were not expelled.
And the men in that group chat? The ones who watched the invitation come in and did nothing? I haven’t heard a word about consequences for them.
Online, the pile-on has already started. Not on the men. On her. She wanted it. She put herself there. She should have known better.
That’s rape culture. Not a slogan. A pattern.
Now let me speak as an instructor.
Here’s the hard truth from the mat. I can teach a woman to fight off an attacker. I cannot teach a woman to fight off an attacker when her brain has been chemically switched off.
Alcohol and ketamine don’t just slow your reflexes. They take away your judgment. Your awareness. Your ability to recognize you’re in danger at all.
Every defense starts in the mind. When the mind is compromised, the defense is gone.
The only tool left is the one that works before you lose it: presence of mind. The ability to notice that something is wrong with you and leave while you still can. I know how close this can come to home. Two stories stay with me.
My daughter was a student at NYU. She was in a friend’s dorm room. Two male students were there. She took a drink. Within minutes she felt herself changing. Something had been slipped into it.
She recognized what was happening. She said she was going to the bathroom. She walked out quietly, called an Uber, and went back to her own dorm.
She did everything right. And I think about that night all the time. If she had waited ten more minutes, if the drug had hit harder or faster, she wouldn’t have had a choice to make. It could have ended very differently. And the people asking questions afterward would have been asking about her drinking.
I know that because of the second story.
One of my students has a daughter at a well-known university in the Southeast. Her daughter’s roommate was raped. When the university investigated, they interviewed my student’s daughter. Every question pointed in one direction. Was her roommate promiscuous? Was she the kind of girl who invited attention?
They weren’t investigating a rape. They were building a case against the victim.
Why would a university do that? Because institutions protect themselves first.
Universities live and die by reputation. Sexual assault numbers hurt enrollment. Headlines hurt donations. So, there is pressure, spoken or not, to shrink the story. Reframe it. Find a reason it wasn’t really what it looked like.
Essays. Workshops. Quiet suspensions. A victim who leaves school while the accused move on. That isn’t justice. That’s damage control.
The law isn’t much better.
New York has what’s become known as the “voluntary intoxication loophole.” Rape charges generally require force or a clear refusal, unless the victim was unconscious or drugged without her consent. If she drank on her own, even to the point where she could no longer say yes or no, prosecutors face a steep climb. The Tompkins County DA pointed to that very law when he explained why no charges were filed the first time.
Think about what that means. The moment a woman takes a drink, the law hands her a share of the blame for whatever is done to her after she can no longer resist. The man who chooses to exploit her incapacity is protected by her choice to have a beer.
That thinking runs deep, and it doesn’t stop at the dorm room door. It reaches into marriage. In 2015, a lawyer for Donald Trump insisted that you cannot rape your spouse. Years earlier, a Virginia lawmaker argued that a husband-wife rape conviction was nearly impossible when a couple shared a bed. These weren’t fringe voices. They were people with power, saying out loud that a woman’s consent can be assumed.
And the imbalance doesn’t stop there. In a number of states, a woman who becomes pregnant from rape has no legal way to end that pregnancy, because the abortion ban makes no exception for rape. In some of those states, the doctor who helps her faces a harsher maximum sentence than many convicted rapists. She carries the consequences. He may never be charged at all.
So where does that leave someone like me?
I’m frustrated. I’ll say it plainly. I’ve spent my career building women’s confidence and capability. I believe in that work, and I’ll keep doing it. But if we measure sexual assault prevention by whether a woman can physically fight off her attacker, we are measuring the wrong thing.
The defense has to start earlier. Before the drink gets spiked. Before the group chat lights up. Before anyone decides a woman’s body is there for the taking.
It starts with men.
“Boys will be boys” is not an excuse. “Locker room talk” is not harmless. Words become thoughts. Thoughts become actions. A culture that shrugs at the words will eventually shrug at the actions. We just watched it happen in a group chat, where one message offered a woman up and nobody stopped it.
So, here’s what I’m asking for.
From the law: close the loophole. Incapacity is incapacity, no matter how it happened.
From universities: stop managing your reputation and start delivering consequences. Expulsion, not essays.
From men: speak up. In the chat. In the locker room. At the party. The bystander who stays silent is part of the system that lets this happen.
I’ll keep teaching women to protect themselves. But I’m done pretending that’s where the defense begins.
It begins with the people who choose to cause harm, and the people who let them.
Gus Bottazzi is Chief Instructor at Krav Maga Personal Safety and author of The Krav Maga Essentials Handbook: A Practical Safety System for College Students; How to Avoid, De-escalate, and Escape Real-World Threats

name: Maryland Matters
title: Poll: Moore sits with a comfortable 2-1 margin over Republican challenger Cox
description: The results are part of a new poll released Tuesday by the Institute of Politics at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County. That poll finds that Moore would pick up 51% of the vote while another 24% said they favor Republican Dan Cox.
text:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox, right, and Gov. Wes Moore (D) will share a stage for their only debate of the election on Oct. 6 on Maryland Public Television. A new poll released Tuesday by the University of Maryland, Baltimore County finds Moore with a comfortable double-digit lead over the Cox. (File photos by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) would cruise to a second term in office if the election were held today, according to a new poll from the Institute of Politics at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County.
The poll, released Tuesday, finds that Moore would pick up 51% of likely voters while Republican Dan Cox was favored by 24%. Another 14% didn’t know, while 11% was divided between other candidates.
“If anything, what’s notable is that sometimes incumbents will pick up an anti-incumbency bias — people who are just sort of frustrated with incumbents in general,” said Mileah Kromer, director of the UMBC Poll. “You’re really not seeing a lot of that here. The numbers very much look like you would expect, given the demographic characteristics of the state and the disproportionate fundraising numbers between the two candidates.”
The poll comes with four weeks left in the campaign season. Nearly 600,000 voters have already received mail-in ballots. Early voting begins Oct. 22 and ends on Oct. 29.
The survey is based on interviews with 776 Marylanders who said they were likely to vote. It was conducted from Sept. 22-27 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5%.
The roughly 2-1 margin is reminiscent of the 2022 race between Moore and Cox. Four years ago, Moore, who had never held public office, trounced Cox by 32 percentage points to become Maryland’s first Black governor.
Third-party candidates decry exclusion from only debate of the governor’s race

Moore and Cox are scheduled to square off Tuesday afternoon in what is expected to be the only head-to-head debate of their rematch. But Todd Eberly, a political science professor at St. Mary’s College of Maryland, said the UMBC poll casts doubt on how much the debate will matter to voters.
“It would be hard for me to imagine anything that could happen in that debate that would alter the trajectory of this race,” Eberly said. “Even if Cox had a fantastic debate performance, I don’t see how he closes that gap, or in any way really improves the clear problem he has winning over Democratic voters.”
Two third-party candidates on the ballot are not included in the Maryland Public Television debate. Green Party nominee Andy Ellis and Working Class Party nominee Cathy White each got 3% in the UMBC survey, below the 10% threshold set by MPT to qualify for the debate.
Moore does best among Democratic voters, 72% of whom said they support the incumbent. Cox picked up three out of every four Republican voters in the UMBC survey, along with 4% of Democratic voters and 14% of the unaffiliated voters.
In Maryland, where Republicans are heavily outnumbered, a GOP candidate running statewide needs to pick up about 90% of the voters in their party, along with roughly three in 10 Democratic voters and more than 55% of unaffiliated voters. It’s a formula that has cracked the door for some successful statewide Republican candidates over the last 20 years.
“Our poll suggests that Dan Cox is not rebuilding the Larry Hogan coalition,” Kromer said, of the Republican governor who served from 2014-2022. “It’s very clear. He’s getting most, almost all the support from Republicans that are his party base. Unaffiliated voters are the required pathway to victory for a Republican statewide candidate.”
Republicans are “running against an incumbent who is polling at 51% in this poll in a Democratic state — an incumbent that, at least according to this, is currently only winning over about three quarters of Democrats,” Eberly said. “That would normally be the recipe for the potential for a Republican to be competitive, and yet they are not competitive at all.”
“Look, Moore is not in danger of losing, but he’s an incumbent Democrat polling at 51%, and the cross tabs show that he’s got 72% of Democrats,” Eberly said. “This is the kind of environment where Larry Hogan showed us Republicans could be competitive in Maryland, and they’re not. I really do wonder, will they get the message, or will they continue to move away from a Larry Hogan-type or even a Bob Ehrlich-type nominee.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Voter perceptions of Cox and his party appear to be factors.
Cox spent four years in the House of Delegates as a conservative firebrand. He once brought articles of impeachment against Hogan for the governor’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. Cox also opposed closures and restrictions on restaurants and other businesses and filed lawsuits on their behalf.
He also closely aligned himself with President Donald Trump, organizing a bus trip to Washington on Jan. 6, the day that turned into a violent political protest at the U.S Capitol.
Efforts by Cox to separate his history from his current political incarnation have not been successful, according to the UMBC poll. Three voters in five identified Cox as conservative or very conservative. Just 11% identified him as a moderate candidate.
In 2018, 47% of those surveyed in another poll conducted by Kromer identified Hogan, in his bid for a second term, as a moderate.
“He’s just not perceived as the type of Republican that Maryland Democrats and frankly a lot of unaffiliated voters are willing to cast the ballot for,” Kromer said. “He doesn’t have the campaign funding to try to make the case that he is a moderate. That’s the path to victory. He doesn’t have the money to do that statewide, or frankly the record to claim political moderation.”
Eberly added that there’s reasons for Democrats to be cautious in the days after the Nov. 3 election.
“Let’s assume Democrats win big,” he said. “The worst thing Democrats could do is interpret a big win as some big endorsement for the Democratic Party. What they should do is realize this is a rejection of the Republican Party, and Democrats were the only other choice on the ballot.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A move to gut Head Start standards
description: Speak up to oppose federal cuts on Head Start rules that will gut its standard of care.
text:
In 2004, as a social worker serving families in deep poverty, I started a diaper bank because many of my clients were unable to afford enough diapers to keep their babies dry and healthy. It was a no-brainer. Head Start already required programs to provide diapers for enrolled children.

Joanne Samuel Goldblum

This gold-standard early childhood program’s regulations included many small but essential items to be in stock for children. This is because long before President Lyndon Johnson established Head Start, he was a young teacher in a Texas border town where families could not afford basic necessities. He wrote his mother heartfelt letters asking her to send toothpaste and toothbrushes for his students.
A proposed federal rule would reduce Head Start’s requirements from 133 pages to about a dozen. That’s not a move to trim red tape but to slash basic standards. No diapers, no formula, no toothbrushes, no class size or staffing ratio requirements.
This follows earlier Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) cuts that have led to closure of some regional offices. Head Start was one of Johnson’s “Great Society” programs, along with Medicare, Medicaid and what we now know as SNAP (Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program).
When I was growing up in the 1960s and 70s, a bipartisan majority in our government believed that all Americans benefitted from a strong social fabric. This was woven of help for seniors who could not afford their doctor bills or workers who had trouble putting food on the table after a factory closure. Nobody wanted to live in a society plagued by anxiety, where one piece of bad luck could cause a downward spiral. We wanted to be able to raise our families in vibrant communities, with parks and libraries, and send them to college, obtainable to working families through student loans.
There was no shortage of exclusion, injustice or want in these years, but there was some recognition that we needed to conquer these evils because Americans shared a common destiny. If some other family’s children were denied the opportunity to thrive, it threatened our common prosperity.
Today all the programs I grew up with that wove a strong social fabric are under attack. The National Diaper Bank Network (NDBN), more than 300 nonprofit basic needs banks across the country, is seeing requests for help reach an all-time high, even exceeding what we faced during Covid.
When Covid-19 was rampant, I was so proud of how NDBN members rose to the moment by organizing drive-through pick-ups for families and expanding to serve people who had never needed to ask for help before. A pandemic, this country can survive. But we will not survive the loss of community, the denial that we all have an interest in making sure that everyone in our society can thrive.
Let me tell you about “Sophia,” the client who convinced me to start a diaper bank in New Haven. I saw her dump the solids out of a diaper and put it back on her baby. I tried not to show my shock and calmly explained that a baby needed a fresh diaper with every change to stay healthy. Sophia told me should could not afford a new diaper every time.
I assumed that there was some government program to pay for diapers, but then, as now, that was not the case. She couldn’t use cloth because she had no washing machine, and the coin laundry would not let her wash diapers. To make matters worse, Sophia’s cash assistance relied on her going to job training. She got a voucher for free child care to facilitate this, but the provider required parents to buy diapers for use while the babies were in care. Sophia couldn’t. She was falling through a gaping hole in the social fabric and at risk of losing the few dollars she got to pay her rent.
Her story, sadly, is far from unique. NDBN research shows that nearly half of young U.S. families struggle to afford the diapers that their children need. Most of the families that NDBN diaper banks serve include working adults, but average pay has not kept pace with expenses. It’s a rigged system that profits those at the top, creates misery at the bottom, and hurts the vast majority of Americans.
 Research shows that when children receive diapers they have fewer pediatric sick visits, creating savings for Medicaid. Giving families diapers protects their access to child care, allowing parents to work more hours and attend school more consistently. Family income rises and so does the amount that the household contributes through taxes. Diapers are also a low-cost intervention to address the maternal mental health crisis. Moms report that diaper insecurity is more stressful to them than food insecurity.
I could go on at length about the social good that arises from the simple act of helping families out with diapers. I encourage people to comment on the disastrous rule proposal to gut Head Start, which we can do through October 6.
More basically, I urge you to speak up about the kind of society you want to live in. In a truly great society, every child has the opportunity to thrive.
Joanne Samuel Goldblum is the CEO at The National Diaper Bank Network in New Haven.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Baltimore can show how to prevent youth homelessness before it begins
description: Any number of problems -- an unexpected expense, loss of transportation, a family fight -- can tip a young person over into homelessness, write Larry Cohen and Tom Coale, but minimal assistance they go into a shelter can help them avoid homelessness.
text:
A homeless encampment is seen in Paterson, New Jersey. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Until very recently, Maryland’s response to youth homelessness kicked into gear only after a young person had already lost a place to live, at the most difficult and expensive point in a housing crisis. But Baltimore is bringing a logical, practical and scalable approach to addressing housing insecurity among young people with a simple proposition: Identifying what would keep a young person housed and providing it before a temporary crisis becomes lasting homelessness.
For many young people, homelessness begins with a specific financial emergency. A family conflict leaves someone without a place to stay. An unexpected expense consumes the money needed for rent. A young parent needs a security deposit. A student loses campus housing or lacks transportation to keep a job.
The amount required to stabilize the situation may be modest compared with the cost and disruption that follow. Yet available assistance is frequently too small, arrives too late or can be used only for an expense that does not match the actual problem.
Point Source Youth’s Targeted Housing Assistance Program was designed around that mismatch. A young person facing an imminent housing crisis works with a trained community provider to develop an individualized housing action plan. The program then supplies a one-time, flexible payment large enough to carry out that plan, whether the need involves rent, utilities, transportation, moving expenses or another immediate barrier to stable housing.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




The model has now produced encouraging evidence. In a seven-state pilot evaluated by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, 345 young people ages 16 to 27 received an average of approximately $3,700, generally within 48 hours, and those funds ended their crisis and slide into homelessness. Including dependents and other household members, the program affected 623 people. Administrative homelessness system records showed that 92.8% of participants had not accessed homelessness services six months after receiving assistance.
Those findings show that rapid, adequately funded assistance delivered before shelter entry merits expansion, and merits investment.
That next phase is underway in Baltimore through Point Source Youth’s partnership with Thread, a local organization with the relationships and community knowledge needed to reach young people before a housing crisis becomes visible to the formal homelessness system. The results in Baltimore will help determine whether the national pilot’s results can be reproduced locally, and what infrastructure is required to sustain the model.
Private funding has made that work possible, but it cannot be the endpoint.
Baltimore City and the state of Maryland should help finance future cohorts and the local capacity required to serve them. That means supporting the payments themselves, along with the outreach, staffing, housing planning and follow-up that make the intervention work. Public partners can also help establish efficient disbursement procedures, strengthen responsible data sharing and support independent evaluation of Baltimore’s results.
Such an investment would be disciplined rather than open-ended. Public officials could examine who the program reaches, how assistance is used, whether participants remain outside the homelessness system and which elements must be preserved as the model grows. Local evidence would then determine the appropriate scale and funding structure.
Maryland is particularly well positioned to do this work. Baltimore has experienced community organizations capable of delivering the program, Johns Hopkins researchers who can continue evaluating it and public leaders who understand that housing instability affects education, employment, health and family stability. This October, Point Source Youth’s national symposium in Baltimore can bring those groups together around a concrete question: What would it take to make prevention a durable part of Maryland’s homelessness response?
The national implications are significant. Communities across the country are searching for ways to reduce homelessness while controlling the cost of crisis systems. A successful Baltimore implementation, backed by credible local evidence and a serious public-sector partnership, could give other jurisdictions a model they can adapt.
Maryland does not need to wait until every question has been resolved. It should invest enough to learn what works while young people still have housing within reach.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland Supreme Court removes Anne Arundel Orphans Court judge from bench
description: The Maryland Supreme Court ordered the immediate removal Monday of Anne Arundel County Orphans' Court Chief Judge Vickie Gipson for what it called "egregious ... misconduct" in office, just months after removing another judge on the same court.
text:
Anne Arundel County Circuit Court in Annapolis. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)The Supreme Court of Maryland ordered the immediate removal Monday of Anne Arundel County Orphans’ Court Chief Judge Vickie Gipson for what it called “egregious … misconduct” in office.
The four-page order came just hours after Gipson pleaded her case to the court Monday, asking it to reject the Maryland Commission on Judicial Disabilities’ recommendation that she be removed from the bench and instead let her serve out the remaining few months of her term and retire.
It’s the latest chapter in an ongoing dispute between Gipson and former Orphans Court Judge Marc Knapp, who was ordered removed from the bench in June for conduct “fundamentally incompatible with judicial office” — conduct that stemmed from a series of run-ins with Gipson. As with Gipson on Monday, the court in July cited egregious misconduct as the reason for Knapp’s removal.
In her comments to the court Monday, Gipson, the first Black chief judge of the county orphans court, touted the improvements to the court during her tenure despite “a concerted effort by some to undermine the process.”
“I understand the seriousness of the court’s review, and ask the court to consider the full record including my conduct, the circumstances under which I served, the steps I took to seek help with resolution and the work that I accomplished on the Orphans’ Court,” Gipson told the justices.
Anne Arundel County Orphans’ Court Chief Judge Vickie Gipson. (Photo courtesy Maryland State Archives)
“I apologize for the strain this matter has placed on the court, the judiciary and public confidence,” she said. “I regret the moments when I could have communicated with greater restraint, or responded to conflict in a more measured way.”
She said she accepted responsibility for her choices, but was “respectfully maintaining my objections to findings I believe are not supported on the record.”
The commission had recommended that Gipson be removed from the bench for a “persistent course of unprofessional action unbecoming of a judicial officer.” The court apparently agreed in Monday afternoon’s order. It said a full opinion would follow at a later date.
The commission said Gipson, who was first elected in 2018, and Knapp, elected in 2022, initially had a cordial working relationship on the three-judge court, but that it quickly turned acrimonious.
The two “engaged in repeated verbal altercations” that were at times “mutual, with both … exhibiting unprofessional behavior to varying degrees and would inhibit the court’s deliberations and cause staff present in or near chambers to be uncomfortable.” These altercations could be heard by court personnel and, occasionally, by the public, the commission said.
Because of her disputes with Knapp, the commission said Gipson tried to refuse to let him submit dissenting opinions and would attempt to bar the court “from issuing orders which had been signed by” Knapp. When he refused to leave the courtroom after one such dispute, she called police to remove him.
The commission said Gipson inappropriately invoked her title as chief judge “in legal proceedings and public statements to advance her personal interests.” It also said she violated court confidentiality in comments to reporters about Knapp, the court and complaints she filed with the commission against other judges, which are confidential.
While she was feuding with Knapp, the commission said Gipson was making accommodations for the third judge on the court, Judge David Duba. Orphans’ court is required to meet at least twice a week, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., but when Duba could not get to court until 11 or later, Gipson allowed for cases to be rearranged around his schedule, inconveniencing the public and workers in the Orphans’ Court and the Register of Wills office who had to work extra hours to accommodate the change.
State Supreme Court removed Anne Arundel Orphans’ Court judge for ‘egregious misconduct’

When pressed by the justices, Gipson said she believed she had the authority as chief judge to rearrange the court schedule and to deny dissenting opinions on the court’s orders. She conceded that she sometimes lost her temper with Knapp, who she felt was threatening, and that she could have sought advice from the commission sooner. But in other areas, like seeking a peace order against Knapp, she said she was just following recommendations from the commission and from police when she expressed concerns about her safety and the safety of others in the office.
“I hope to leave the court with my head held high, not because I believe I am flawless, but because I served with commitment, I learned from this experience and I made a meaningful contribution to the court and the people it served,” she told the justices.
But Kendra Jolivet, the attorney for the commission, said that Gipson’s actions merited removal from the bench because they violated court rules and “impaired court functionality, public access and the administration of justice.”
“The respondent [Gipson] devotes large portions of her exceptions to alleging institutional hostility, bias, racial tension or past disagreements with colleagues,” Jolivet told the justices. “Even if accepted as true, none of these allegations justify altering court operations without consensus, they don’t excuse inappropriate conduct toward colleagues and staff or negate the cumulative seriousness of the misconduct found.”
The commission found that while Knapp was the “primary aggressor in the underlying interpersonal conflict,” that does not outweigh the “gravity and breadth of respondent’s sanctionable conduct.”
In its unsigned order, the Supreme Court said it found that Gipson “committed one or more of the violations” charged by the commission and that “based on the egregious nature of the misconduct in this case, removal … is the appropriate disposition,” to take effect immediately.
Gipson did not run for reelection this year, in deference, she said, to the court and the charges against her. With her removal Monday, none of the three judges elected to the orphans’ court in 2022 remain on the bench. In addition to Knapp being removed this summer, Duba resigned in November 2024.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Michele Tafoya hopes national Republicans put money behind their praise
description: LE SUEUR — Michele Tafoya has TV skills and an opponent saddled with the state’s fraud scandal. What she needs now is money. Polls show Tafoya is in a dead heat with Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, even with significant national political headwinds forcing Republicans to spend heavily in traditionally red strongholds such as Iowa, […]
text:
Republican Senate candidate Michele Tafoya appears at a campaign event with Senate Majority Leader John Thune in Le Sueur, Minn. on Oct. 5, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)LE SUEUR — Michele Tafoya has TV skills and an opponent saddled with the state’s fraud scandal. What she needs now is money.
Polls show Tafoya is in a dead heat with Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, even with significant national political headwinds forcing Republicans to spend heavily in traditionally red strongholds such as Iowa, Alaska and Kansas.
At a campaign stop with farmers on Monday in Le Sueur, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., boasted that Tafoya is a strong candidate with a convincing message to give Republicans hope for winning in a state they’ve mostly surrendered.
But he was noncommittal on deploying some of Senate Republicans’ vast war chest to boost Tafoya’s campaign before the Nov. 3 election. Fox News reported in August that the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Thune, and allied groups had raised more than $500 million for the midterms thus far.
“We’ve got a big map this year. It’s a very competitive environment,” said Thune, who’s touring battleground states. “But Minnesota is unique in a lot of ways.”
Tafoya has a strong pitch to make that she can be the first Republican to win a Senate seat in Minnesota since 2002. She has high name recognition from her successful career as a sports reporter on virtually every major television network. She isn’t bogged down with any major personal scandals besides frequently bashing Minnesota and threatening to decamp to Florida. And her opponent is an easy target to hammer on the fleecing of the state’s generous safety-net programs, which unfolded during her two terms as No. 2 in state government.
“I think we can make a very strong case out of all these Senate races … This is one worth investing in,” Tafoya said. “We’re going to talk. We haven’t had that conversation yet.”
Money isn’t everything, as Flanagan showed when she trounced U.S. Rep. Angie Craig in the Democratic primary despite being far outspent.
Monday’s stop at the Pfarr family’s farm — 4,000 acres of corn, soybeans, alfalfa, peas and hogs about an hour southwest of Minneapolis — was Tafoya’s first open press event since the August primary.
After a private roundtable with farmers organized by the Minnesota Farm Bureau, Thune and Tafoya briefly addressed the press to promote Republicans’ work on a farm bill and reaffirm their commitment to passing year-round E15 fuel, which would be a boon for corn growers whose crops become ethanol.
GOP Senate candidate Michele Tafoya reports assets totaling $10.7M to $37.9M

Farmers have been whipsawed by President Donald Trump’s trade war, which hurt grain exports, and war with Iran, which drove up fuel costs.
Nevertheless, many farmers are sticking with him, and the Minnesota Farm Bureau endorsed Tafoya for Senate.
Flanagan held an event at a gas station in Brooklyn Park on Monday with Minnesota Farmers Union President Gary Wertish to draw attention to high fuel prices, though it hardly needed pointing out. Gas station signs are serving as a kind of campaign ad for Democrats across the country.
Matthew Pfarr, whose family hosted Tafoya, approached the current state of affairs with equanimity. He said farmers face ups and downs no matter which party controls the government.
“So, farmers have gotten quite good at weathering those,” Pfarr said.
Asked whether he was backing Tafoya, Pfarr demurred.
“We will host anyone who wants to come to the farm,” Pfarr said. “I prefer not to discuss my politics, personally.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Grand Island-area lawmaker reflects on Trump’s visit to central Nebraska
description: GRAND ISLAND, Neb. — One of two state lawmakers representing Grand Island in Nebraska’s one-house Legislature praised President Donald Trump for visiting the area Monday. Trump’s rally was at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Legislative District 35, represented by state Sen. Dan Quick of Grand Island. The fairgrounds are one block away from Legislative Dist[...]
text:
Merchandise for sale on the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, ahead of a campaign rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)GRAND ISLAND, Neb. — One of two state lawmakers representing Grand Island in Nebraska’s one-house Legislature praised President Donald Trump for visiting the area Monday.
Trump’s rally was at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Legislative District 35, represented by state Sen. Dan Quick of Grand Island. The fairgrounds are one block away from Legislative District 34, represented by state Sen. Loren Lippincott of Central City. Quick is a Democrat; Lippincott is a Republican. The Legislature is officially nonpartisan, meaning lawmakers do not officially organize by political party and lawmakers’ party affiliation doesn’t appear on the ballot.
State Sen. Loren Lippincott of Central City holds up a sign reading “I’m Billy Bob!” referring to comments made by registered nonpartisan Senate candidate Dan Osborn in reference to Red Cloud, Nebraska residents, in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds ahead of a midterms rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Lippincott told the Nebraska Examiner inside the Pinnacle Bank Expo Center that Nebraska is “very honored” to host Trump. Lippincott stretched his arms to thousands gathered Monday as proof “Nebraskans are absolutely thrilled” for the president of the United States to come.
“We’re very excited here in Grand Island,” Lippincott said. “Not only do we have the State Fair, but then to be selected for a Trump rally is just absolutely spectacular. We are totally thrilled about it.”
In 2025, Lippincott led the effort to restore Nebraska’s “winner-take-all” Electoral College model. Nebraska currently awards two Electoral College votes to the statewide winner and one vote for each of Nebraska’s three congressional districts. Two Republicans buckled. Had all of the Legislature’s 33 Republicans unified, the measure could have passed the 49-member body.
But on Monday, Republicans sought a different message behind Trump as thousands came dressed in red, some in sequins and others in clothing they’d made to honor Trump. Trump won Hall County, which includes Grand Island, with 65% of the vote in 2016, 66% in 2020 and 68% in 2024.
“We know that this part of the state is red already, so it’s not like he’s coming here just to pick up a lot of votes, but instead, it’s to honor the individuals that do support his agenda and do support the work that he has done, which has been substantial,” Lippincott said. He said some of the biggest accomplishments for Trump are around public safety, in crime rates and immigration.
State Sens. Bob Hallstrom of Syracuse, left, and Dan Quick of Grand Island. Jan. 7, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Quick, a Democrat, has twice outperformed Trump in the three times both have been on the ballot in the district. In 2016, Quick won with 50.3% of the vote.
But in 2020, Quick handily lost reelection — 53.6%-46.4% — to former state Sen. Ray Aguilar of Grand Island. Aguilar had previously served from 1999-2009. Quick staged a rematch in 2024 and won with 50.3% of the vote again. That race was the most expensive in direct spending for legislative races in 2024, with nearly $670,000 between Quick and Aguilar. Quick outspent Aguilar by $84,000.
Quick, one of the more moderate Democrats in the Legislature, said in a text that he had meetings in Lincoln on Monday. He declined to comment on Trump’s visit.
Some Nebraska Democrats, such as Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb of Hastings, have said Trump’s 2026 midterms tour is a sign of weakness. Kleeb encouraged an “unwelcoming committee” for Trump on Monday and said on social media that Trump’s visit “tells you one basic fact: Republicans are in trouble, even in Nebraska.”
Trump asks Nebraska to ‘pretend’ he’s on the midterm ballot

Other Trump critics have scrutinized possible local costs for security and law enforcement overtime. Lippincott hailed Falls City agribusinessman Charles Herbster, who announced he would pay those costs.
Furthermore, Lippincott said he expected the rally to boost Grand Island’s economy by increasing sales and lodging tax revenue.
On Republican vulnerability, Lippincott offered a different view from critics such as Kleeb. He said Trump has a “forehead of flint, and whenever he finds any kind of resistance, he runs headlong into it.”
“In my opinion … these kinds of rallies are like what the sunshine is to Superman,” Lippincott said. “It restores his strength. He loves this type of arena, this type of environment, and this recharges him.”

Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) clashed in a war of words and protest signs in downtown Lansing on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, during a pair of demonstrations calling out Lawrence and Barrett over their respective campaign planks — and in the case of Barrett, his congressional record — with just 31 days left in the 2026 general election cycle. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Members of “Spartans for Will,” who back Democrat Will Lawrence, and supporters of Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) clashed in a war of words and protest signs in downtown Lansing on Monday evening during a pair of demonstrations calling out Lawrence and Barrett over their respective campaign planks — and in the case of Barrett, his congressional record — with just 31 days left in the 2026 general election cycle.
Lawrence, the Democratic nominee for the 7th Congressional District, and Barrett, the seat’s incumbent, are set to square off Tuesday in a debate hosted by WKAR-TV in Lansing.
Organizers of the pro-Lawrence demonstration, which was held outside of Barrett’s office in Lansing, called attention to the congressman’s record on artificial intelligence, the data centers that power its proliferation, healthcare and other issues that progressives have noted in their calls to elect Lawrence in the fall.
Camden Kimmel, a Michigan State University student and a member of “Spartans for Will,” gave remarks at the protest, highlighting the group’s issues with Barrett. Cynthia Burton, with Bee Accepting, also aired grievances with Barrett’s time in office.

“We must act now. Status quo systems, policies, and politicians are never going to fix the damaging mistakes of the past two, 12, 20, 189 and 250 years. The opportunity to unite people towards a better future is here, and we will not let it pass us by,” Kimmel said. “I very much consider Tom Barrett a status quo politician. Taking corporate PAC money, bowing down to Trump and voting for the ‘Big Beautiful Bill,’ supporting the war in Iran, and entrenching our energy grid’s dependence on the fossil fuel industry. He has expressed no desire to stand up to AI startups and data center builders, instead preferring to pass that responsibility over to the local townships.”
Lawrence spokesperson Mya Legel told Michigan Advance following the event that “Michiganders have paid the price of Tom Barrett’s cost- raising record in Congress.”
“One night on a debate stage is too little, too late to make up for two years of absence, billionaire tax breaks, and rubber-stamping Donald Trump’s agenda,” Legal added.
Barrett’s supporters counter-programmed the protest by holding one of their own, calling out Lawrence’s associations with the democratic socialist movement, his arrest record from days of protesting oil pipelines, and other grievances with Lawrence’s campaign.
Several members of the pro-Barrett demonstration were asked if they would like to be interviewed by the Advance, but declined. Those present and representing Barrett at the counter-demonstration included members of the the Michigan Republican Party, from GOP legislative aides to members of regional and county GOP offices.
A message seeking comment from Barrett’s campaign was not returned at the time of publication. This story will be updated when a response is received.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Trump asks Nebraska to ‘pretend’ he’s on the midterm ballot
description: Trump vist to Nebraska was just one stop for the president on a midterm campaign blitz to shore up red states.
text:
President Donald Trump headlines a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)GRAND ISLAND — President Donald Trump told the crowd in Grand Island Monday to pretend that he is on the ballot this November. 
Trump, during his rally speech at Pinnacle Bank Expo Center, announced an executive order that allows anyone to use red-dyed diesel, waiving the off-road requirement and allowing anyone to purchase it for any reason.
Trump said the order should “assure” Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts and Gov. Jim Pillen of reelection. 
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen announces he has inducted President Donald Trump as the newest “admiral” of the largely honorific Nebraska Navy in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds for a midterms rally featuring the president. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
It’s been roughly 20 years since the last presidential visit to Grand Island. Then-President George W. Bush visited in 2006, during the tail end of that year’s midterm election campaign. Former Gov. Ben Nelson won another term in the U.S. Senate against Ricketts that year. 
Ricketts, now a U.S. senator, is in a bitter race against nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn. The Ricketts campaign was handing out signs saying “I’m Billy Bob!” and “I’m Mary Jane!” — referring to Osborn’s comments about hypothetical Red Cloud Trump supporters.
The Trump visit comes as the political environment for Republicans has worsened. Nebraska was just one stop for the president on a midterm campaign blitz to shore up red states.  Before Trump went on stage, Ricketts hit his campaign-trail classics when talking about his opponent, calling Osborn a Democrat and mentioning audio leaks and Osborn paying his family for campaign work. 
Ricketts, in a joke he often tells on the campaign trail, asked the audience to vote 10 times but not the “Democrat way,” meaning he wants them to bring along people they know to vote. 
“We will keep Nebraska red,” Ricketts told the crowd.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

Trump jokingly said both Ricketts and Pillen are always asking for money for the state. Trump followed Ricketts’ lead, calling Osborn a “fake independent,” adding that Ricketts is a true warrior. Trump also mentioned Democratic gubernatorial challenger Lynn Walz, saying she is related to Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, whom he called probably the worst governor ever. 
Lynn is related to Tim Walz through her husband, who is a distant cousin. 
U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., greets thousands of Nebraskans gathered in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds for a midterms rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The president highlighted his record — blaming “fake news” for people not knowing about his successes — and touted the tax cuts from his “big beautiful bill,” a secured border and the economy. 
“We were a dead country a few years ago. … Now we’re the hottest country ever on that,” Trump told the crowd. 
Trump went on to say that the U.S. is kicking “Iran’s ass.” The president added that higher gas prices are just a small price to pay. 
“[Iran] can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles or San Diego. This is a very small price to pay. It’s essentially almost over with,” Trump said.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilger, 3rd District Rep. Adrian Smith, Pillen and Ricketts spoke before Trump took the stage.  
The Osborn campaign released a statement thanking Trump for announcing his support for “right to repair” laws and for expanding access to red-dyed diesel.
Walz, in a campaign statement, said, “Political attacks won’t lower anyone’s property taxes or reopen a single market for our farmers. Nebraskans deserve a governor whose word actually means something. I’m ready to show up for you.”
The Nebraska Democratic Party held a protest near the venue. The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting has already started.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Roger Marshall’s attack ad against Adam Hamilton contains unauthorized image of children
description: U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall's commercial critical of Democrat Adam Hamilton features unauthorized use of a picture taken of youth sitting in a Kansas chapel.
text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall's latest reelection campaign ad critical of Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton makes unauthorized use of an image of children sitting in a chapel at a Linwood camp. The camp's leaders insist Marshall remove the photo from the ad that opens with a picture of Marshall leaning on a fence. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Marshall's campaign commercial)TOPEKA — The Tall Oaks Camp and Conference Center demanded Monday that U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall suspend a campaign commercial attacking Democrat Adam Hamilton that made unauthorized use of a photograph of children at Tall Oaks’ chapel in Linwood.
A senior advisor to the Marshall campaign said the ad was “corrected,” but hours after that statement was issued, a version of the commercial available on social media still included an image of the Tall Oaks’ distinctive chapel and about two dozen people sitting on pews.
Lea Ann Combs, president of the board of directors at Tall Oaks, a nonprofit summer camp and retreat center, said Tall Oaks wasn’t consulted by the Marshall campaign and didn’t approve inclusion of the photograph in the commercial. The ad denounced Hamilton in relation to allegations of sexual abuse perpetrated by a volunteer at Church of the Resurrection, the prominent Johnson County-based church founded and led by Hamilton.
“Our concern is straightforward,” Combs said. “This advertisement creates a misleading association between Tall Oaks, the young people pictured and events that did not happen here. Protecting the dignity of these young people and accurately representing our organization should be a shared priority.”
She said Marshall’s campaign should stop broadcasting the 30-second commercial until confirming the Tall Oaks photograph had been deleted.
The commercial began airing in conjunction with reports on a decision by the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican super PAC, to pull $8 million from a North Carolina campaign and redirect it to help Marshall’s reelection bid in Kansas. The latest New York Times/Siena College Poll shows Hamilton and Marshall tied at 45% support each, based on a survey of likely voters.
In the ad paid for by Marshall’s campaign, a photograph of the senator appeared in the opening sequence while a recording of his voice said he approved content of the commercial. The senator’s ad claimed Hamilton didn’t respond promptly to a report suggesting a church volunteer may have touched or attempted to touch boys attending a 2005 program hosted by Church of the Resurrection.
“Parents were ignored and Hamilton never called police,” Marshall’s attack ad says. “He should never be our senator.”
The commercial included still photos of Marshall and Hamilton, cottages, dormitory-style rooms, hiking trail, rural property and a group of people sitting in rows, most with their back turned, in the chapel at Tall Oaks.
Combs said permission had been granted to photograph young people at Tall Oaks for the purpose of promoting the camp and its programs. She said that approval didn’t extend to inclusion of photographs in political campaign advertising, particularly commercials delving into claims of sexual abuse. Tall Oaks works to provide a safe environment for children, families, faith communities and other organizations using its facilities, the statement said.
The statement said Tall Oaks encouraged Marshall to remove the photograph from all platforms tied to the campaign. The objective was to make certain no one viewing the ad would mistakenly believe Tall Oaks or the children appearing in the ad were connected to allegations of abuse, the statement said.
The request shouldn’t be interpreted as an endorsement or rejection of any candidate or a comment on the merit of allegations raised in the commercial, the statement said.
Brent Robertson, Marshall’s chief of staff, said the photograph from Tall Oaks was thought to have been a “stock image” available for general use. The Tall Oaks picture wasn’t taken at the site of Hamilton’s “child molestation cover-up,” Robertson said.
“The image has already been corrected and, luckily, Kansas families care far more about Hamilton’s failure to protect kids from a child sex predator than what cabin picture was used,” Robertson said.
Tyson Brody, a campaign spokesperson for Hamilton, said the ad wasn’t in line with Marshall’s vote in September 2025 to block a U.S. Senate measure directing the U.S. Department of Justice to release unclassified records about Jeffrey Epstein. The wealthy financier, child sex offender and acquaintance of President Donald Trump committed suicide in 2019 while awaiting trial on charges of sex trafficking of minors.
“Marshall lies and uses children as political pawns to distract from the fact he had pregnant mothers arrested and jailed over small medical debts, and voted to protect the predators named in the Epstein files. Roger Marshall is desperate to hide from his record of protecting predators, and preying on low-income families in Kansas,” Brody said.
In a Kansas Reflector report published in July on abuse allegations involving Church of the Resurrection, Hamilton said two church employees conducted an internal investigation into claims that surfaced in 2005. The inquiry was inconclusive, Hamilton said, because the children couldn’t identify the perpetrator.
Hamilton said he should have forwarded information to law enforcement rather than depend on church staff. When new allegations surfaced against volunteer Scott Moore in 2006, the church informed police of allegations associated with camp retreats in 2005 and 2006.
Moore was accused of sex crimes in the Kansas City area and Massachusetts. He was convicted in 2013 in Kansas of a misdemeanor count of sexual battery. In 2015, Moore was found unconscious after he fled police when caught half-naked in a car with a teenage boy. He died at a hospital.
Tall Oaks is a nonprofit camp, retreat and conference facility on 236 acres near Linwood.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Feds approve $150 million for second power link between Interior and Southcentral Alaska
description: The U.S. Department of Energy said on Monday that it has approved $150 million to partially fund a second electrical intertie between Southcentral Alaska and the Interior. When built, the Beluga-Healy Transmission Project would result in a redundant power link between Fairbanks and Anchorage, increasing the ability of power companies to use the cheapest elec[...]
text:
A high-voltage power line is seen on Sept. 4, 2018, in Alaska. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)The U.S. Department of Energy said on Monday that it has approved $150 million to partially fund a second electrical intertie between Southcentral Alaska and the Interior.
When built, the Beluga-Healy Transmission Project would result in a redundant power link between Fairbanks and Anchorage, increasing the ability of power companies to use the cheapest electricity possible, even if it’s coming from the opposite end of the railbelt.
Construction isn’t expected until after 2030.
The project is expected to cost $418 million altogether, with the new federal money likely going toward engineering, planning and permitting, said Curtis Thayer, executive director of the Alaska Energy Authority.
The remaining $268 million could come from other federal grants, the state, or even AEA itself, through loans. 
AEA has been planning the second intertie for almost five years as part of a broader campaign of electrical upgrades across the state but didn’t intend to go ahead until other parts of that campaign — including high-voltage links to support a newly renovated Bradley Lake hydroelectric project — came online.
On Monday, Thayer said the announcement came as a surprise. He had heard last week that the state was in the running for a large grant through a Department of Energy program intended to benefit defense readiness, but he didn’t know until Monday that AEA had won.
Alaska’s existing intertie was built in the 1980s and is used primarily for shipping lower-cost hydropower and natural gas power north to Fairbanks. In recent years, it has also been used to ship coal-fired power south to Anchorage amid natural gas shortages.
Adding a second intertie increases the amount of power that can flow north or south, something that could encourage the development of wind or solar power plants that could provide cheaper power, albeit intermittently.
A second link also means that when the first intertie is upgraded and replaced — something intended in a separate project — power will continue to flow across the railbelt. 
Monday’s grant comes from the Defense Production Act and $1 billion approved by Congress and President Donald Trump for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security.
Most of Alaska’s military bases use energy that flows through the intertie, and the state’s Congressional delegation emphasized that fact as it lobbied for federal funding.
On Monday, the three members of the delegation — Rep. Nick Begich III and Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan, all Republicans — issued statements in support of the new grant.
Sullivan and Begich are running for re-election this year, and on Monday, Vice President J.D. Vance was scheduled to travel to Fairbanks in order to campaign for both men, as well as other Republicans seeking office in November’s general election. According to Reuters, Vance was expected to speak about the grant during a rally at Fairbanks International Airport.

name: Daily Montanan
title: District Court judge rules birthdate voter law unconstitutional
description: A Lewis and Clark County District Court judge has ruled a law requiring voters to put their birth year on absentee ballots violated the state’s constitution, and has ruled in favor of Disability Rights Montana and Big Sky 55+, which challenged the legislation. Ballots for the Nov. 5 general election have already been sent overseas, […]
text:
Lewis and Clark Courthouse is pictured on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026, in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)A Lewis and Clark County District Court judge has ruled a law requiring voters to put their birth year on absentee ballots violated the state’s constitution, and has ruled in favor of Disability Rights Montana and Big Sky 55+, which challenged the legislation.
Ballots for the Nov. 5 general election have already been sent overseas, with voter packets headed to Montanans by the end of the week. Some overseas ballots have been sent and returned. 
In a statement, the Secretary of State’s Office said county election officials have been notified that the courts have blocked House Bill 719 and expressed frustration with the ruling.
“This type of mass confusion is why courts shouldn’t get involved when the election is underway,” Secretary of State’s Office spokesperson Richie Melby wrote in an email.
The Montana Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment or say if it planned to appeal the decision. 
The court’s decision also invalidates the law, meaning a ballot couldn’t be thrown out simply for not having a voter’s birth date on the ballot. When asked if any ballots would be reprinted, the Secretary of State’s Office said it takes counties “weeks” to contract with printing companies and get the ballots ready for mailing.
“The law requires that absentee ballot materials were available to voters for in-person absentee voting beginning today,” Melby said Monday. “The election is well underway.”
Three elections have been held under the new law, with data submitted to the court showing more ballots have not been counted since the new law has been in effect. The court compared voter data from the November 2024 election, which was before the new birth date law, with an all-mail May 5, 2026, election that was held in 30 counties after it was signed into law.
Lewis and Clark County’s ballot rejection rate was 0.29% in 2024 and 0.8% in the May 2026 election. In Gallatin County it rose from 0.47% in 2024  to 2.75% in 2026, court documents state.
The state argued adding the birth year helped prevent voter fraud, with attorneys pointing to a case where another person voting in Montana impersonated his ex-wife in 2011. 
“Balanced against the state’s lack of evidence of election fraud and its inability to explain how public confidence in elections is elevated by requiring a birth year on absentee ballots, the state has failed to meet its burden of proving HB 719 is reasonable and serves a legitimate state interest or that its asserted interests are more important than the burden on the right to vote,” Judge Mike Menahan wrote in his decision.
In a press release, Big Sky 55+ praised the decision.
“The court’s decision means that no Montanan will have their ballot thrown out for arbitrary reasons under HB719,” Terry Minow, chairperson of Big Sky 55+, said in a press release. “When more people vote and have their votes counted, our democracy is healthier. We encourage everyone to vote in every election.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Bank of North Dakota announces stablecoin pilot program with local partners
description: MEDORA, N.D. – The Bank of North Dakota announced Monday it has launched a pilot program for its Roughrider Coin.  Four local banks and credit unions are using the state’s unique banking model, led by the Bank of North Dakota, to learn about possible benefits and pitfalls of the stablecoin financial technology.  “The way money […]
text:
Don Morgan, center-right, CEO of the Bank of North Dakota, announces the launch of a stablecoin pilot program with four local partners during a banking forum at the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora on Oct. 5, 2026. The chair of the state-owned bank's advisory board, Karl Bollingberg, center-left, joined Morgan on stage alongside nearly two dozen people who have been involved in the Roughrider Coin's development.  (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)MEDORA, N.D. – The Bank of North Dakota announced Monday it has launched a pilot program for its Roughrider Coin. 
Four local banks and credit unions are using the state’s unique banking model, led by the Bank of North Dakota, to learn about possible benefits and pitfalls of the stablecoin financial technology. 
“The way money moves is drastically changing, and we are utilizing our incredibly powerful financial tool to be on the forefront of that change,” said Don Morgan, CEO of the Bank of North Dakota. “We believe it will benefit the state over the next decade in huge ways.”
Bank of North Dakota to launch state’s first stablecoin known as Roughrider coin

The state-owned bank will partner with Gate City Bank, First International Bank, Capital Credit Union and North Star Community Credit Union on the pilot program to test stablecoin in a controlled environment. Fiserv, a Fortune 500 technology company that already provides services for the Bank of North Dakota, is also part of the partnership. 
Roughrider Coin is North Dakota’s branded stablecoin. Stablecoin is a form of cryptocurrency because it uses blockchain technology to complete transactions. But it doesn’t experience the same value fluctuations of cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin because stablecoins are tied to the value of the U.S. dollar.
“Stablecoin at its very foundation is pegged to the dollar, and $1 of stablecoin is going to be worth $1. It won’t be worth $1.10 the next day,” said Bob Herrington, CEO of North Star, a credit union that started in Benson County and now has 13 locations. “Its use, because of that, is not one of investment and appreciation but it’s a transactional use and it is more secure because of the blockchain technology.”
Herrington said North Star wanted to be part of the pilot program because the credit union wants to be prepared down the road if stablecoin becomes an essential tool in the world of financial technology.
“Right now, the impact to everyday member or customer base transactions is very, very far down the time horizon,” Herrington said. “If you don’t start here, you’re not going to be prepared for the next phases of stablecoin.”
Ryan Goellner, executive vice president of Gate City Bank, said he hopes the Roughrider Coin will create efficiencies in how the bank operates. But he and bank leaders are still evaluating its potential uses and view the pilot program as a learning opportunity.
“Participating in the Rough Rider Coin pilot really gives us an opportunity to learn firsthand in that controlled environment, rather than kind of just waiting on the sidelines,” Goellner said. “The focus right now is just really for us to get that understanding of the stablecoin and then how we can actually utilize it internally.”
North Dakota bankers cautiously optimistic about stablecoin announcement, though future risks exist

The pilot program’s announcement was made at the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora during a three-day forum the Bank of North Dakota is hosting for the state’s banking leaders to learn more about financial technologies like stablecoin. 
Morgan said the bank has completed its first live transactions outside of a test environment by using the stablecoin to move a penny almost instantly between two partners. He said the occasion is the start of a foundational change in the banking world, similar to the moment when an automobile first replaced a horse-drawn carriage. 
“That’s the importance of today because North Dakota is on the forefront of that,” Morgan said.  
Karl Bollingberg, chair of the Bank of North Dakota’s advisory board, said he believes stablecoin could have ramifications on a similar scale to the advent of internet banking. 
Bollingberg said he remembers how complex it was when the bank’s leaders first approached him about what would become Roughrider Coin. 
“It was a bit like listening to someone speak underwater. You knew that they were saying something. Just had no idea what,” Bollingberg said, adding he’s grateful the Bank of North Dakota is providing education for banking leaders. 
North Dakota moves forward with stablecoin as local banks express interest in pilot project

The Roughrider Coin is not available for use by the general public or merchants. The pilot program is designed to test bank-to-bank transactions behind the scenes. Morgan said the Bank of North Dakota chose to limit the scope of the pilot program to minimize the potential risk of the new financial technology early on. The bank’s internal and external risk assessments concluded the initial Roughrider Coin program would be considered low risk.  
Banks typically use existing systems like ACH or wire transfers to move money from one bank to another. But these systems take time to complete a transaction, especially when crossing international borders. The systems also have daily deadlines that can create difficulties and cost money. 
“If we miss the cutoff by even a few minutes, it’s going to have to go out the next morning. Whereas if I used Roughrider Coin to do that same transaction, they’re gonna get it while I’m on the phone with them, telling them it’s coming,” Herrington said.
The Bank of North Dakota hopes the Roughrider Coin will become a faster and cheaper alternative to traditional payment methods. But to what extent it will complement or replace those existing payment methods depends on a lot of factors. It’s something the bank hopes to learn more about during the pilot program. 
“I’d be shocked if this doesn’t have a high rate of adoption and a high rate of transactions fulfilled within it,” Morgan said. “But there are a lot of unknowns still.”
North Dakota banking customers should not see any immediate changes or impacts even if their financial institution is involved in the pilot program. Long term, Morgan said one of the first benefits customers could potentially see is pushing daily transaction deadlines later in the day.
“There could potentially be quicker transaction times when that gets rolled out to the client level,” Morgan said. “You could see that as one of the first kind of benefits to occur.”
Ag commissioner lukewarm on Bank of North Dakota’s foray into stablecoin

Morgan said the Bank of North Dakota plans to add more banks and credit unions in the state to the program over time. There is no set deadline for the pilot program. 
“We’re not getting in any hurry. We have no rush to market. We’re not trying to meet shareholder return expectations. We’re trying to build this very safely, thoughtfully,” Morgan said. “If this pilot went on for a whole ’nother year of simply just testing and working out kinks and bugs, I would be OK with that.”
The Bank of North Dakota will provide regular updates to the North Dakota Industrial Commission, a three-person board chaired by Gov. Kelly Armstrong, which oversees the bank. One member of the commission, Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring, has urged the bank to proceed with caution.
