name: Delaware
title: Delaware puts another $7.1M into early literacy — now comes the results test
description: Bridge to Practice grants emphasize phonics, teacher coaching and classroom instruction as Delaware tries to turn science-of-reading policy into measurable gains for students. DOVER, Del – Delaware is investing another $7.1 million in early literacy instruction, expanding a statewide effort aimed at moving science-of-reading training from policy manuals and[...]
text:
Bridge to Practice grants emphasize phonics, teacher coaching and classroom instruction as Delaware tries to turn science-of-reading policy into measurable gains for students.
DOVER, Del – Delaware is investing another $7.1 million in early literacy instruction, expanding a statewide effort aimed at moving science-of-reading training from policy manuals and professional development sessions into everyday classroom practice.
The Delaware Department of Education announced Monday that 28 school districts and charter schools will receive Bridge to Practice grants for the 2026-27 school year.
The grants support Delaware’s Birth through Grade 3 Early Literacy Plan through teacher training, instructional materials, classroom coaching and school leadership development.
It is the second round of Bridge to Practice funding. A first round announced in March awarded $6.1 million to 25 districts and charter schools, bringing the two-round investment to about $13.2 million.
The approach addresses one of public education’s persistent challenges: Passing a law, adopting a curriculum or training teachers does not necessarily improve student achievement unless those changes reach the classroom.
“We know how to teach children to read, and we believe every Delaware student can become a strong reader,” Education Secretary Cindy Marten said.
Marten said policy, resources, training and coaching are important, but none should be confused with the ultimate goal.
“The work is making sure what we know reaches students through strong instruction every day and then showing our progress in ways we can reliably measure, see and report,” she said.
Phonics returns to a central role
The science of reading reemphasizes phonics as a key part of early reading instruction while placing it within a broader research-based approach to literacy.
Phonics explicitly teaches children how letters and combinations of letters correspond to sounds in spoken language, giving beginning readers the tools to decode unfamiliar words rather than relying primarily on context, pictures, or guessing.
The broader science-of-reading approach also includes phonemic awareness, fluency, vocabulary, oral language, background knowledge and comprehension.
The goal is not simply to help children sound out words, but to build the foundational decoding skills they need to read accurately, understand what they read and continue building knowledge over time.
The new grants support science-of-reading professional development programs including LETRS and AIM Pathways, curriculum-based professional learning, Student-Centered Coaching and leadership development through the Early Literacy Leadership Academy.
Local flexibility brings local responsibility
Districts and charter schools can use the funding differently based on local needs.
Appoquinimink School District used earlier funding to strengthen literacy leadership and relationships between principals and instructional coaches. Capital School District connected LETRS training with classroom reflections, student work and coaching. Indian River School District focused on greater consistency among elementary schools through instructional frameworks, classroom learning walks and science-of-reading training for pre-K through third-grade educators.
That flexibility gives local school leaders room to determine how best to implement the state’s literacy goals rather than requiring every district to follow exactly the same model.
But greater discretion also places more responsibility on local school boards to determine whether those investments are working.
Julia Keleher, executive director of First State Educate, has repeatedly argued that local boards are where state education policy becomes action.
“State strategy becomes real for students when local leadership brings it to life,” Keleher said. “Boards will the grant money to deliver results as measured by improved reading proficiency and then use data to guide decisions, monitor implementation and hold school the school leaders accountable.
Keleher has also emphasized that this new grant adds to the responsibility already resting with local boards to get results.
That responsibility becomes particularly important in early literacy and grants structured like this one.  School boards help determine whether interventions succeed by approving staffing, budgets, and accountability structures.  In practical terms, boards are being asked not only to approve literacy programs and spending, but also to establish measurements, examine whether those investments are producing results, and hold district leaders accountable for increasing the number of students reading at grade level.
Spending must translate into readers
Delaware’s reading performance remains a significant challenge.
About 40% of Delaware third-graders reached proficiency in English language arts in 2026, leaving a majority of students below grade-level proficiency.
That makes the next stage of the literacy initiative as much an accountability test as an instructional one.
DDOE said it will examine classroom walkthroughs, coaching cycles, implementation measures and student literacy data throughout the school year.
Those measures can help determine whether schools are implementing the program as intended.
But training sessions, coaching visits, new materials and completed professional-development programs are inputs.
The ultimate outcome is whether more children learn to read proficiently.
Guarding against another permanent program
The increased emphasis on evidence and classroom results is encouraging, but the state will also need to guard against allowing Bridge to Practice to become another permanent education funding stream regardless of performance.
Government programs created to address urgent problems can become difficult to unwind after districts build staffing, contracts and budgets around them.
That makes measurable results especially important.
If districts receiving the grants show meaningful improvements in reading, the state will have evidence that continued investment is producing value.
If student performance remains stagnant after repeated rounds of funding, Delaware should be willing to reconsider the strategy, redirect resources or require changes in how the money is being used.
The program should not be judged successful simply because it continues to operate.
Largest grants approach $1 million
The largest award this year is $877,624 for Red Clay Consolidated School District.
Capital School District will receive $763,856, Christina School District will receive $652,691, Appoquinimink School District will receive $556,457 and Colonial School District will receive $556,167.
Milford School District will receive $248,238.
Awards range from $9,528 for Gateway Charter School to nearly $878,000 for Red Clay.
Those differences reflect the size and needs of participating school systems, but the larger grants also create a reasonable expectation that taxpayers should eventually be able to see what changed as a result of the investment.
That does not mean every district should produce identical results. Student populations, staffing and local circumstances vary considerably.
But the state and local boards should be able to demonstrate a connection between taxpayer investment, improved classroom instruction and student academic growth.
An accountability clock starts ticking
Delaware’s early literacy strategy rests on a reasonable premise: Children who become strong readers during the earliest grades have a much better foundation for success throughout school.
The decision to emphasize evidence-based reading instruction, restore phonics to a central role and help teachers translate their training into daily classroom practice is a defensible use of education funding.
But after approximately $13.2 million in two rounds of Bridge to Practice grants, Delaware is moving beyond the stage where implementation alone can define success.
Marten’s own standard provides the appropriate test: Progress should be something Delawareans can measure, see and report.
Keleher’s argument adds another layer to that standard: As boards gain greater responsibility for directing resources, they also assume greater responsibility for measuring results and holding their own district leadership accountable.
The state has identified the problem, adopted an approach and committed significant resources.
Now the test is whether those decisions produce more students reading at grade level.



TO GO BOX

Who: 28 school districts and charter schools will receive funding for the 2026-27 school year.
Why: The money supports science-of-reading instruction, including a renewed emphasis on phonics, teacher coaching, instructional materials and school leadership.
Total investment: The latest grants follow $6.1 million awarded in March, bringing the two rounds to about $13.2 million.
What to watch: Whether teacher training and classroom changes produce measurable increases in student reading proficiency — and whether funding remains tied to results rather than becoming a permanent program.

title: Arkansas lawmakers adopt recommendations for per-student school funding
description: The Joint Education Committee recommended Monday that Arkansas increase the per-student funding directed to public schools by more than 2% over the next two years.  Schools would receive $8,239 per student for the 2027-2028 academic year and $8,431 the following school year, under the recommendations advanced Monday. Schools currently receive $8,037 per stud[...]
text:
Rep. Keith Brooks (left) and Education Secretary Jacob Oliva present the LEARNS Act to the House Education Committee on Feb. 28, 2023. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)The Joint Education Committee recommended Monday that Arkansas increase the per-student funding directed to public schools by more than 2% over the next two years. 
Schools would receive $8,239 per student for the 2027-2028 academic year and $8,431 the following school year, under the recommendations advanced Monday. Schools currently receive $8,037 per student. 
The proposed increases will go before the Legislature during the legislative session, which begins in January.
Arkansas Explained: How is the state’s public school funding amount set?

The recommendations are the culmination of a months-long adequacy study that occurs every other year and is the result of school funding litigation. 
The Legislature is required by law to recommend the amount of state funding needed to provide an adequate and equitable education, and provide a report of their recommendations to the leaders of the House and Senate by Nov. 1. 
Committee co-chair Rep. Keith Brooks, a Republican, said lawmakers are recommending $1,000 for dyslexia intervention services for students in kindergarten through 3rd grade, representing about $26 million in new spending next year. 
The committee’s recommendations also include $14 million for high-cost occurrence students. High-cost funding applies to individual cases where costs associated with special education and related services required by an Individualized Education Program are unduly expensive, extraordinary or beyond the routine special education and related services, according to the state education department.  
Brooks said these changes represent about $40 million in new dedicated special needs funding next year.
“These recommendations, they’re not just strong, they’re amongst the strongest this committee’s ever made in the history of the adequacy study, including giving a strong credence to the concern over special needs funding with significant funding there,” he said. “So I’m proud of the work we’ve done.” 
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, including Republican Rep. Julie Mayberry, expressed concerns about receiving the recommendations at Monday’s meeting and not having more time for discussion before voting on them. 
“I’m very happy to see a lot of the things that are in here, I really am, I just wish that we had a little bit more overall discussion because I don’t think this committee has had that chance to have those discussions,” Mayberry said.  
Rep. Stephen Meeks, a Greenbrier Republican and senior member of the committee, said this is not the end of the discussion. The recommendations are needed to draft legislation and lawmakers can continue to debate the amounts proposed in that legislation when the session starts in January, he said.
Brooks said he plans to run a bill proposing the new per-student funding amounts during next year’s session.

text:
(Main photo by simpson33 via iStock / Getty Images Plus; seal courtesy State of Iowa)The Iowa Supreme Court has suspended for 90 days the license of a Johnson County lawyer who admits he cannot properly account for his use of clients’ money.
The Iowa Attorney Disciplinary Board has alleged that attorney Michael Ralph Brown admits having failed to maintain the proper client-account reconciliations, monthly lists of individual client balances, journals of receipts and disbursements, bank statements and other financial records.
Due to the lack of records, an auditor could not determine whether the more than $80,000 remaining in Brown’s client trust account consisted of money that “needed to be returned to clients” or was money representing earned fees belonging to Brown, the board alleged.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The board, in recommending that the Iowa Supreme Court suspend Brown’s license for 90 days, noted that Brown “has taken responsibility for his misconduct and fully cooperated with the board.”
However, the board added, Brown was admonished by the state’s Client Security Commission in 2021 for violations similar in nature to the more recent case, demonstrating “a failure to learn” from past mistakes.
In addition, the board said, Brown’s recordkeeping deficiencies were “so severe,” they “demonstrated a near total loss of accountability for client funds.” That situation was aggravated, the board said, by Brown’s decision to destroy files in preparation for closing his office and retiring.
The Iowa Supreme Court followed the board’s recommendation and recently ordered that Brown’s Iowa license to practice law be suspended for 90 days. The suspension may have little practical effect in that Brown retired from practice prior to the order being issued, according to state records.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Brown for comment but in recent court filings, Brown stated that he has had to undergo a number of medical procedures in recent years, including a pacemaker implant, that have caused profound fatigue. He told the court that while his condition is not an excuse for his conduct, it has been a “small contributing factor to my inability to properly look after my law practice.”
Iowa Judicial Branch records currently list Brown’s 90-day suspension as stemming from both “disciplinary” action as well as a “disability.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Legislature looks to limit lay use of the title ‘nurse’
description: New legislation would expand the prohibition on representing oneself as a nurse to include the generic term, rather than just licensed positions.
text:
New legislation would expand the prohibition on representing oneself as a nurse to include the generic term, rather than just licensed positions. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)An Assembly panel unanimously approved legislation that would fine individuals who call themselves nurses without holding the proper licenses.
Nurses told the Assembly Regulated Professions Committee, which unanimously approved the bill, the change is needed to help maintain trust in nurses, though some witnesses urged steeper fines and other changes that would bar chatbots from identifying themselves as nurses.
Margaret Farrell Daingerfield, president of the New Jersey State Nurses Association, told lawmakers that nurses are held to strict regulatory requirements that ensure that they can competently assess the health of the patients, administer treatments, and make critical decisions in high-stakes environments.
“When individuals without this training use this title, it blurs the line between qualified professionals and unlicensed personnel,” she said.
Those blurred lines could create confusion that risks patient safety, Daingerfield said, adding it also risks eroding trust in the profession broadly by allowing unlicensed individuals to represent themselves as healthcare providers.
Though existing law already bars lay people from representing themselves as registered nurses, advanced practice nurses, and licensed practical nurses — including through their abbreviations — it does not place the same restriction on the title “nurse.”
The difference between a licensed provider and someone representing themselves as a nurse isn’t always readily apparent, Daingerfield said.
A niece who had hired a “baby nurse” did not realize the individual was not a licensed nurse until her mother, who is a nurse, came to visit, Daingerfield said.
Daria Waszak, executive director of the New Jersey Collaborative Center for Nursing, asked the committee to consider raising existing fines for misrepresenting oneself as a registered, advanced practice, or licensed practical nurse. Those are set at $200 for a first offense and $500 for subsequent missteps.
And she said lawmakers should bar artificial intelligence chatbots from calling themselves nurses to prevent consumers understand when they are speaking to an actual nurse.
“Regardless of where it is, any setting where health interactions take place, it is very important that it remains clear to a consumer when they are interacting with a licensed human nurse and they are not,” Waszak said.
The bill has no Senate companion.
 Midwives
The panel also unanimously approved legislation that would create a new board to license midwives who are presently overseen by the State Board of Medical Examiners. The board also licenses doctors, physician assistants, and other healthcare professionals.
Midwives provide reproductive healthcare, including labor assistance, within or outside of a hospital. Some are licensed as nurses in addition to the midwifery licenses they need from the Board of Medical Examiners.
A more specific licensing board would be better able to assess the work of midwives, said Mia Leong, a midwife at the Haledon-based Rowan Birth Services.
“The people responsible for setting standards for midwives should understand the work that midwives actually do and the specific needs of the communities that we serve,” she said.
Multiple midwives urged the panel to add language saying midwifery is distinct to healthcare and to remove language that would require midwives to carry professional liability insurance, arguing that requirement could be financially ruinous.
Insurance requirements would be better left for regulators or a separate bill, said Vicki Hedley of the New Jersey Certified Professional Midwives Association.
“The bill creates an insurance mandate without creating a corresponding mechanism to ensure that appropriate and affordable professional liability coverage is actually available to the midwives who would be licensed under the act,” she said.
Only one New Jersey insurer offers liability policies to midwives, Hedley said.
The Senate advanced a companion bill through the Senate Commerce Committee in June, but the two versions are not identical, and it’s unclear how their differences will be reconciled.

title: Bobby Charles’ campaign returning contributions that exceeded limit amid ethics complaint
description: Republican gubernatorial nominee Bobby Charles’ campaign acknowledged Monday that it accepted contributions that exceeded the limit, and is in the process of refunding them, according to campaign manager Dale Crafts Jr. Meanwhile, the Maine Ethics Commission is reviewing a complaint by the Maine Democratic Party which claimed Charles’ campaign knowingly acce[...]
text:
Bobby Charles, the Republican gubernatorial nominee in Augusta on June 23, 2026. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star) Republican gubernatorial nominee Bobby Charles’ campaign acknowledged Monday that it accepted contributions that exceeded the limit, and is in the process of refunding them, according to campaign manager Dale Crafts Jr.
Meanwhile, the Maine Ethics Commission is reviewing a complaint by the Maine Democratic Party which claimed Charles’ campaign knowingly accepted donations exceeding $2,075. The commission has not determined yet whether Charles or his campaign violated the law.
The Maine Democratic Party said in a press release Monday that it found 46 contributions to Charles’ campaign that exceeded $2,075, totaling more than $25,000. The release also said Charles had been ordered by the commission to return funds to donors. Jonathan Wayne, the commission’s executive director, clarified that there has been no determination of wrongdoing yet.
“We have asked the Charles campaign to use information (compiled by commission staff) to conduct its own investigation into whether it accepted over-the-limit contributions,” Wayne told Maine Morning Star.
“If the campaign concludes that it has, we ask that the campaign rectify the situation by returning the excessive amounts to the contributors,” Wayne continued.
He added that the Republican nominee’s campaign had agreed to those terms. 
A Maine Morning Star review of Charles’ campaign finance records found 39 individual contributions over the limit, including at least three that were double the permitted maximum. Some of those were reported twice on the same day, leaving it unclear if they were erroneously duplicated. 
Crafts said that the errors were likely due to couples contributing through the same check instead of individually, or people over-donating because they didn’t realize that fees were included.
“It’s as simple as that, some people donated too much, and it should have been dealt with before the filing, essentially,” Crafts said. He said the complaint, which comes weeks before the election, is politically motivated.
The Maine Democratic Party’s complaint is the only instance of a campaign finance probe against a 2026 candidate for governor this year. Wayne said the commission occasionally finds that a candidate has accepted an over-the-limit contribution, “but it does not happen often.”
In a letter sent to the campaign treasurer on Friday, Wayne wrote that commission employees will send their assessment of any potential contributions that exceed the limit to Charles’ staff, and will expect a written response by Oct. 16. At the upcoming Oct. 26 commission meeting, the commission will determine any potential finding of violations or penalties.
“It’s premature for the commission staff to make any predictions or recommendations about that,” Wayne’s letter said. 
However, in the Maine Democratic Party’s complaint, it asked the commission to look at Charles’ entire campaign finance history that extends beyond the latest filing period. 
“If Bobby Charles can’t follow Maine’s campaign finance laws as a candidate, Mainers have every right to question why they should trust him to follow the law as governor,” a statement from spokesperson Lauryn Fanguen said.
Fanguen also pointed out that while campaigns may receive donations over the limit, the fact that Charles’ campaign waited until a complaint was filed to return the money is evidence of wrongdoing.
“We’re glad they’re returning the funds,” she said. “They should have done that before we filed a formal complaint.”

text:
Early in-person voting runs Oct. 15-31, 2026 in North Carolina. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)If you are planning to vote in the midterm elections, there are some very important deadlines coming up. The first deadline is 5 p.m. this Friday, Oct. 9, which is the voter registration deadline.
If you are eligible to vote, you can complete your registration online or in person at the N.C. Division of Motor Vehicles.
You also have the option of filling out the registration form and delivering it or mailing it back to the N.C. State Board of Elections. It’ll be accepted as long as it is postmarked by Oct. 9.
Early in-person voting begins on Thursday, Oct. 15. If you missed the Oct. 9 registration deadline, you can still take advantage of same-day registration during early voting.
Unlike on Election Day, during early voting you can vote at any location in your county. You can look up early voting locations here. Early in-person voting will wrap up at 3 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 31.
If you’d like to see your sample ballot before you go to vote, you can look it up here.
More absentee ballots in NC in danger of being tossed under new directives

If your plan is to vote by mail, Tuesday, Oct. 20 is the deadline to request an absentee ballot. And it must be received – not postmarked – by your county Board of Elections office no later than 7:30 p.m. on Election Day in order to be counted.
If you requested an absentee ballot but worry it may not arrive in the mail by Election Day, you are still allowed to vote in person. Election officials simply ask that you discard the unused absentee ballot and not return it to the Board of Elections to avoid confusion.
If you’ve changed your address recently or wish to change party affiliation, click here to learn how to update your voter registration. You can also make changes to your registration in person if you use early voting.
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Polling sites are open from 6:30 a.m. until 7:30 p.m. statewide. You must go to your assigned voting site to make sure your vote will count. Click here to find your Election Day polling place.

name: VTDigger
title: Despite some overall progress, Vermont test scores show a widening achievement gap
description:
The state’s initial evaluation of its annual standardized test scores shows a widening gap between marginalized students and others. The Vermont Agency of Education says the state’s school funding model is to blame. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Despite some overall progress, Vermont test scores show a widening achievement gap.
text:
A classroom. Photo via Adobe Stock

Despite some improvements in standardized test scores, state data reveals a widening achievement gap in Vermont’s schools. 
The state’s initial evaluation of its annual standardized test scores for the 2025-26 school year, released last month, shows “marginalized students,” including those with disabilities, living in poverty or belonging to a racial minority, are falling behind their peers.
The gap in subject matter proficiency between students who are considered marginalized and those who are not ranges from 30 to 38 percentage points, according to data from the Vermont Agency of Education. 
And that gap has only grown over time, according to Education Secretary Zoie Saunders. Last year’s evaluation showed gaps ranging from 26 to 36 percentage points between marginalized students and their peers depending on the subject matter. 
The results come as lawmakers and Gov. Phil Scott are in a multi-year effort to radically change public education in Vermont, starting with consolidating the state’s school districts and transitioning to a new education funding model. 
Alongside Scott, Saunders has advocated for moving the state to a foundation formula method, which provides districts with a set amount of money based on their number of students and how expensive those students are to educate. Currently, districts have wide latitude to build their budgets from the ground up.  
Saunders said that the widening statewide disparities are evidence that Vermont needs the transformation she envisions, which she said will provide more equitable resources, leading to better outcomes for students. 
While advocates agree that disparities are fueled in part by gaps in resources, they say the problem isn’t so easily attributed to solely school funding. 
Rebecca Eunmi Haslam, a professor of education at St. Michael’s College who specializes in racial equity, said the state needs to better support students of color by, for example, improving staff responses to bias. 
Schools need to ask: “What do we do when students are experiencing bullying and harassment at school? What do we do when our curriculum does not reflect their experiences or their reality?” Eunmi Haslam said. 
The widest disparity is seen in English language arts scores among students in sixth grade, with a 38 percentage point gap between marginalized and non-marginalized students.
The data shows more narrow disparities among students in third and fourth grade who tested in English language arts, with marginalized students scoring 33 points lower than others.
In Saunders’ eyes, the widening achievement gap is evidence that the state’s education system and the funding model that scaffolds it need reform. 
“Our current funding system is not equitable, and it’s resulting in a widening between the haves and have nots,” Saunders said. 
In some subject areas, the majority of Vermont students lack proficiency, although the state data also shows modest improvements. For example, only 41% of Vermont students in third through ninth grade on average are considered proficient in mathematics. 
Historically marginalized students make up 57% of students out of the about 80,000 enrolled in the state, according to Grace Fischer, director of the agency’s assessment division. 
The state considers students marginalized if they belong to a racial or ethnic minority, are living in poverty, have an individualized education program, are a migrant or English language learner, are experiencing homelessness, are in foster care or come from a military-connected family.
Karen Price operates an education tip line for the Vermont Family Network, an organization that advocates for kids with disabilities. Parents reach out to the organization for help when things have gone wrong for their child in school, giving her anecdotal evidence of how kids with disabilities can go underserved. 
To Price, the heart of the issue is the fact that special education is often “siloed” from general education, meaning there isn’t a coordinated approach between general education teachers and special educators. 
That separation comes in part from school culture, she said. Sometimes general educators don’t see students with individualized education programs as their responsibility to educate, she said, while other times they don’t properly coordinate with special educators. 
“In a perfect world, the special educator should be able to look at the curriculum and adapt or modify according to the child’s needs,” Price said. 
But that requires advance planning, which doesn’t always happen in the state’s understaffed schools, according to Price. Other times, special educators may not have the expertise to individualize curriculum to students’ needs, she said. 
Gaps are often exacerbated in small schools, she said, because students with disabilities might be in smaller numbers, making it harder for districts to find the qualified supports.
In Saunders’ eyes, gaps in student achievement are the product of Vermont’s education funding system, which allows for a wide range of per-student spending across the state. 
Under the state’s current education funding system, local school boards have the power to decide their districts’ budgets, as long as voters approve. Local property taxes then reflect the local district’s budget, as well as the spending decisions made across the state. 
Saunders has supported transitioning to a foundation formula model, which most states across the country use. Under that model, the state decides how much money it will spend per student, with rates adjusted for those who have high needs. 
Transitioning to a foundation formula model is the key to making more equitable investment across the state’s education system, Saunders said, which would “elevate quality” and make progress closing the state’s achievement gap. The state is set to transition to the new model in 2029 as long as a number of contingencies are met. 
Modest improvements in state test scores are “promising,” Saunders said.  
Proficiency in English language arts among students in third through ninth grade improved by 1.14 percentage points on average compared with 2025, according to the state’s data. 
The state saw more significant improvement in mathematics, with proficiency among students in third through ninth grade improving by 2.7 percentage points on average. 
Saunders attributed the progress to the success of the agency’s recent campaigns to improve student performance in reading and math. Those campaigns involved training teachers on new methodology for teaching the subjects. 
Eunmi Haslam said gaps in the state’s test scores signal that Vermont schools need to be more willing to invest in professional development training to make classroom curricula more inclusive and help staff respond to discrimination. 
Kids of color are more likely to be bullied or feel socially isolated, especially those in rural districts with a mostly white student body, she said. 
“If students aren’t socially well and not emotionally safe, they’re not actually available for academic learning at all,” Eunmi Haslam said. 
But if staff are trained on racial equity, they’re less likely to act on stereotypes and racial bias, creating a more inclusive learning environment, she said.
“People’s first instinct is often to blame the students for failing within the systems that we have set up,” Eunmi Haslam said.
 “We’ve known it’s not working, and we continue to do the same thing.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: US Supreme Court orders another look at how WA political maps are drawn
description: The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday set the stage for another redrawing of Washington state’s political maps. On the first day of its new session, the court accepted a legal challenge to the boundaries, then remanded it to a lower court to determine if the way a federal judge drew the lines in 2024 complies […]
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday set the stage for another redrawing of Washington state’s political maps.
On the first day of its new session, the court accepted a legal challenge to the boundaries, then remanded it to a lower court to determine if the way a federal judge drew the lines in 2024 complies with a ruling earlier this year in a Louisiana redistricting case.
Monday’s action will not affect next month’s election. But it could lead to the state’s legislative district boundaries changing before they’re next scheduled to be redrawn in 2031, depending on the pace at which the process proceeds.
Those contesting the 2024 map and the state attorney general had each asked the Supreme Court to take this step. 
This case dates back more than four years. It started when a group of Latino voters contested the 15th Legislative District borders adopted by the state’s redistricting commission and approved by the Washington Legislature in early 2022.
Their lawsuit contended the final map violated the federal Voting Rights Act because it impaired the ability of Latino voters in the Yakima Valley to participate equally in elections. The case included a trial in June 2022 featuring testimony from commissioners and voting experts.
Plaintiffs argued that while Latinos were a slight majority of the district’s voters, the final contours included areas where their turnout is historically lower and excluded communities where Latinos are more politically active. This fracturing can depress Latino turnout and weaken their voting strength, they argued.
U.S. District Court Judge Robert Lasnik agreed, approving new lines in early 2024 to enhance the political voice of Latino voters. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld his decision, concluding race was not the predominant factor in shaping the redrawn map.
The controversial revamp shifted more than 300,000 people across 13 legislative districts in eastern and western Washington.
Jose Trevino and state Rep. Alex Ybarra, R-Quincy, have sued to get the redrawn maps tossed. They petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court in January to take up the case and were energized in April when the legal landscape was transformed by the Supreme Court in Louisiana v. Callais.
In that ruling, the majority rewrote how the federal Voting Rights Act is applied in redistricting by significantly curtailing the use of race in drawing boundaries. Now, it is expected that Lasnik, first appointed to the bench by President Bill Clinton, will be deciding if his 2024 decision aligns with the court’s current approach.
“The lower courts should be given the first opportunity to apply that decision to the facts of this case,” Washington Attorney General Nick Brown wrote in a brief filed in June.
He noted that would be in line with how the Supreme Court dealt with redistricting cases in Alabama, North Dakota and Mississippi.
Attorneys for the original plaintiffs in the case wanted the Supreme Court to deny the petition. 
“We won this case twice already, and we intend to win again. As a result of our previous litigation, Latino voters in Yakima Valley had an equal voice in state legislative elections for the first time in decades,” Annabelle Harless, director of redistricting at the Campaign Legal Center, said in a statement.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont can help keep Canada close
description:
As tariffs push Canadian businesses toward other markets, Vermont can use its ties to Quebec to its own advantage.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont can help keep Canada close.
text:
This commentary is by Al Vigier, the chief executive officer of Caseway, an artificial intelligence company that co-creates products with large enterprises and shares the revenue with them.
At the Haskell Free Library and Opera House, the border between Vermont and Quebec runs through the reading room. For more than a century, Canadians could walk along a short sidewalk to the front door in Derby Line. Since October 2025, that sidewalk has been closed to most users, except people with reduced mobility. Canadians now use an entrance on Church Street in Stanstead. The library still serves both communities. Getting there has become more complicated.
I run Caseway, a 15-person AI company in Vancouver, British Columbia. We’re a long way from Derby Line, but I recognize the problem. On Sept. 22, we gave up a place in a Canadian government accelerator in Silicon Valley. We were one of eight companies selected from 137 applicants. For a business our size, turning down meetings with potential customers was a difficult call.
We also had to look beyond those meetings. Washington has imposed 50% tariffs on selected Canadian goods and declined to extend the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, although the agreement remains in force. It has also directed federal officials to remove Canadian products from the General Services Administration’s purchasing schedules. That makes it harder to plan an American expansion.

READ MORE

Our two large American customers are staying. We’re directing new growth toward Canada, Europe and Taiwan. We sell software to defense and regulated customers, and we need some confidence about the conditions we’ll be working under.
I don’t need to explain to Vermonters why the Canadian relationship matters. Families and businesses along the border live it. What may be less visible is how companies make decisions while that relationship is under strain.
A canceled ski trip can be rebooked. A business expansion takes longer to undo. Once a company has hired people, signed a partner and learned a new market, it has reasons to keep investing there. Better relations with Washington would be welcome. They wouldn’t erase the work already done elsewhere.
There are opportunities worth pursuing. Canada’s agreement under Europe’s Security Action for Europe defense financing program gives eligible Canadian suppliers access to joint procurement. Taiwan is seeking international partners in its drone industry. We have reasons to spend time in those markets beyond our frustrations with the United States.
Gov. Phil Scott has been clear about his opposition to punitive tariffs on Canada. In July, he warned about the costs to Vermonters and called for stronger economic and cultural ties. From this side of the border, that matters.
Vermont’s congressional delegation can keep pressing for the tariffs and federal procurement restrictions on Canadian products to be reversed. Local employers can help make the case by explaining what these policies mean for their costs, suppliers and plans to grow.
State officials can also use Vermont’s relationship with Quebec. The two governments already cooperate on practical problems, including reducing phosphorus pollution in Missisquoi Bay. Business introductions, clear information about procurement opportunities and regular meetings with small companies would give that relationship more everyday value. A company weighing its next market needs someone who can answer its questions and make a useful connection.
The communities around the Haskell have found a way to keep sharing their library. Vermont can bring that same effort to its Canadian business ties. Policy may improve. By then, some companies will have committed their next few years elsewhere. The time to stay in touch is while those decisions are still being made.

title: We’re making a tough call on an upcoming U.S. House debate
description: Over the past few weeks, the four of us here at the Beacon have been wrestling with a pretty tough decision, and we’d like to get your feedback. A few months ago, Jeff Landfield of the Alaska Landmine asked us if we’d be willing to help with an AARP-sponsored candidate debate. The Beacon would co-host […]
text:
Republican U.S. House candidate Nick Begich, left, and Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska (right) remove their microphones after a televised debate Thursday night, Oct. 10, 2024, in Anchorage. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)Over the past few weeks, the four of us here at the Beacon have been wrestling with a pretty tough decision, and we’d like to get your feedback.
A few months ago, Jeff Landfield of the Alaska Landmine asked us if we’d be willing to help with an AARP-sponsored candidate debate. The Beacon would co-host a U.S. House debate, and the Anchorage Daily News and the Anchorage Press would co-host debates with the candidates for U.S. Senate and governor.
At the time, we thought the benefits clearly outweighed any drawbacks. Earlier this year, we asked you what we should ask candidates for office this year, and a debate is a great way to do that directly — we’d get to ask the U.S. House candidates exactly what you wanted.
Locally, ABC/FOX would broadcast the debate, and C-SPAN would share it nationally, informing voters across the state and country.
We drafted an impartial list of questions inspired by the issues you raised with us earlier this year, including the cost of living, fisheries and President Donald Trump’s performance in office.
The Alaska Beacon on its own doesn’t have the video production capability or event management experience to do a good job on a debate alone, on short notice — especially not without sacrificing some news coverage — so a partnership made sense.
Collaborations are part of our mission to connect Alaskans to their state government, and we partnered with the Anchorage Daily News, Alaska Public Media and KTOO on our voter guides this year. 
But in the weeks since we finalized our partnership with the Landmine, we’ve heard from some readers who say the debate agreement is a bad idea. 
You’ve told us that you believe Alaska Landmine isn’t a journalistic outlet, and Jeff’s advocacy for President Donald Trump and Ballot Measure 2 makes him far from impartial. 
In addition, you’ve told us that Jeff’s decision in 2021 to republish boudoir photos of someone who is now a candidate for governor — photos that had been public on a photographer’s website — went over the line.
Some things have also changed behind the scenes. When we agreed with the Landmine weeks ago, Republican Rep. Nick Begich III had not filled out our candidate questionnaire for the primary election and this would be our first chance to get answers to your questions. He’s now completed one for the general election, and it went online Monday.
Right now, we’ve heard feedback from a relative handful of readers about the debate, but we think that as it becomes better known, more of you will speak up.
And so, after hearing you and thinking about it for a week, we’ve decided to cancel.
We’ll have other opportunities to ask candidates the questions you wanted us to ask. We follow the Citizens Agenda on election reporting — the idea that we ask the questions that are on your minds — and to us, that also means changing course when our readers ask us to.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: U.S. Supreme Court justices appear skeptical of allowing Boulder climate lawsuit to proceed
description: The U.S. Supreme Court’s conservative majority Monday appeared broadly sympathetic to fossil fuel companies’ argument that allowing two Colorado local governments to sue them over climate change in state court would be a “recipe for chaos.” Attorneys for both sides in Suncor v. Boulder, along with the Trump administration, presented oral arguments in a two-h[...]
text:
An aerial view of a Boulder County neighborhood that burned in the Marshall Fire, on Dec. 31, 2021. (Hart Van Denburg/CPR, pool)The U.S. Supreme Court’s conservative majority Monday appeared broadly sympathetic to fossil fuel companies’ argument that allowing two Colorado local governments to sue them over climate change in state court would be a “recipe for chaos.”
Attorneys for both sides in Suncor v. Boulder, along with the Trump administration, presented oral arguments in a two-hour hearing, the first of the Supreme Court’s 2026-27 term. The case originated in Colorado in 2018, when Boulder’s city and county governments sued Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy, seeking monetary damages under state tort law for their role in contributing to climate change.
Despite being filed eight years ago, the case has yet to proceed to trial, as the fossil fuel companies have repeatedly tried to have it dismissed or moved to federal court by arguing that the Constitution and federal clean-air laws preempt such state-level proceedings.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As justices waded into a thicket of jurisdictional issues raised by Suncor and Exxon when they petitioned the nation’s highest court to weigh in last year, Chief Justice John Roberts noted the “practical matter” of what could happen nationwide if Boulder’s case is allowed to proceed.
“Presumably if you prevail, the next day, a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit, probably copy your pleadings, and then there’ll be at least 50 … causes of action filed,” he told the attorney representing Boulder. “How would you think that will work out on the ground?”
Boulder, fossil fuel companies face off at the Supreme Court in high-stakes climate case

With more than 30 similar lawsuits already filed by state and local governments across the country, environmental advocates say the outcome in Suncor v. Boulder could be a turning point in efforts to hold the fossil fuel industry accountable for climate change.
Justice Elena Kagan, the most senior of the court’s three liberal justices, compared the wave of climate litigation to state-level efforts against tobacco companies in the 1990s and against opioid manufacturers in the 2010s. She asked the attorney for Suncor and Exxon if those lawsuits should have been preempted, too.
Kannon Shanmugam, representing the companies, said the tobacco litigation involved “a more traditional misrepresentation claim” and consumers “suffering injury quite directly.”
“I’m waiting to see the distinction,” Kagan replied. “Because this complaint talks a lot about misrepresentations that are made by the defendants.”
Climate change in Colorado
In a statement Monday, Boulder County said that its case seeks to hold the companies “responsible for knowingly contributing to climate alteration while concealing the dangers of their products.”
The Suncor v. Boulder proceedings come after another unprecedented summer of record heat, extreme drought conditions and destructive wildfire activity impacting Boulder and other Colorado communities, as human-caused climate change, mostly the result of fossil fuel combustion, pushes average global temperatures to dangerous new highs. In December 2021, Boulder County was the location of the Marshall Fire — the most destructive fire in Colorado history, and one in which scientists say climate change was a factor.
“Faced with these rising costs, we ask, is it fair for communities to shoulder these costs alone? We believe it is not,” Boulder County’s statement said. “For decades, the companies producing and selling fossil fuels knew that their products contribute to a changing climate. These companies are asking the Court to help them evade responsibility.”
Alito absent
Absent from Monday’s oral arguments was Justice Samuel Alito, one of the Supreme Court’s most conservative members. Alito recused himself from further proceedings in the case last week, after environmental advocates had called for him to step aside because he owns stock in at least two oil companies.
Alongside the two parties to the case, Sarah Harris, U.S. deputy solicitor general, appeared before the court on the Trump administration’s behalf, asking the justices to side with the fossil fuel companies. In an unusual move, the administration filed an unsolicited brief in support of Suncor and Exxon’s initial petition to the court shortly after it was filed in August 2025.
“We agree with petitioners: interstate air pollution is an inherently federal area, and Congress hasn’t authorized this suit in the Clean Air Act,” Harris told the justices.
Though he posed multiple questions to Shanmugam about the companies’ legal arguments, conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh appeared to agree, saying that the court had multiple precedents making it “crystal clear” that issues involving interstate air and water pollution are subject to federal preemption.
“We don’t have to reinvent the wheel,” Kavanaugh said. “Because we’ve said this multiple times — and Congress, presumably, when doing the Clean Air Act and doing the Clean Air Act amendments, has relied on this court’s precedents, establishing that this kind of pollution is a federal law matter.”
Attorney Kevin Russell, representing Boulder, reiterated that the plaintiffs’ case against Suncor and Exxon goes beyond an attempt to merely regulate greenhouse gas emissions.
“The deception claims, I think, are far outside anything the Clean Air Act is designed to deal with,” Russell said. “The Clean Air Act doesn’t give the EPA authority to figure out what is the ideal amount of emissions … or the right mix of fuels, or the right level of economic activity. It is a much more precise mandate that is limited to putting a cap on the amount of emissions from particular point sources.”
But both Kagan and Roberts sounded skeptical of Boulder’s position that its litigation isn’t seeking to regulate emissions.
“Everything depends on this idea that the defendants are responsible for excessive emissions,” Kagan said.
“Isn’t your suit an attempt to evade those (Clean Air Act precedents)?” asked Roberts. “It’s an effort to reduce emissions. The fuel production itself doesn’t have the sort of universal harm that we’re talking about.”
As Monday’s hearing began in Washington, climate activists gathered at a rally in Boulder, where Mayor Aaron Brockett, survivors of the Marshall Fire and other speakers urged the Supreme Court not to issue a ruling that lets the fossil fuel industry off the hook.
“Our community and many others have suffered terribly from worsening wildfires, floods and drought because of the deception of big oil companies, who knew that burning fossil fuels would overheat our planet, but chose to obfuscate the truth to prioritize their profits,” Micah Parkin, an advocate with climate group 350 Colorado, said in a statement. “Boulder deserves to have our day in court to hold these corporations accountable for the costs our community is having to bear.”

title: West Virginia Supreme Court to hear arguments in school vaccine case
description: The West Virginia Supreme of Appeals will hear oral arguments in a court case that may decide the future of the state’s school strict vaccine requirements. In an order entered Monday, justices say they will set a date to hear the state school board’s appeal of Raleigh County Circuit Judge Michael Froble’s November 2025 ruling […]
text:
A nurse administers a vaccine dose at the Ellis R. Shipp Public Health Center in West Valley City on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The West Virginia Supreme of Appeals will hear oral arguments in a court case that may decide the future of the state’s school strict vaccine requirements.
In an order entered Monday, justices say they will set a date to hear the state school board’s appeal of Raleigh County Circuit Judge Michael Froble’s November 2025 ruling prohibiting schools from enforcing the school vaccination requirements on those seeking a religious or philosophical exemption
States generally require that public and private school students be vaccinated for a number of infectious diseases, including polio, measles and chickenpox. West Virginia has been one of only five that do not allow religious or philosophical exceptions to those requirements. Last year, Gov. Patrick Morrisey established religious exemptions by executive order. He has not rescinded the order despite lawmakers in 2025 voting down a bill that would have inscribed them in law. 
Froble’s ruling is on hold as the Supreme Court prepares to consider the case. 
The case was filed by Raleigh County parents Carley Hunter and Miranda Guzman against the Raleigh and West Virginia boards of education, over the school leaders’ refusal to allow their children to attend with a religious exemption. 
Each side will have 20 minutes to present their arguments, unless the court specifies otherwise. Attorneys representing Morrisey will be given five minutes of the respondents’ 20 minutes to participate in the oral arguments, the order says. 
The clerk of the court will notify counsel in the case of the date of oral arguments, the order says.

title: U.S. Supreme Court declines to take up Maine lobster boat tracking appeal
description: The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear a Maine lobsterman’s legal challenge to an electronic vessel tracker requirement, putting an end to the multi-year lawsuit.  In an order Monday, the court denied a request to take up the appeal by Frank Thompson, a Vinalhaven lobsterman.  In a statement, Maine Department of Marine Resources Commissioner Carl […]
text:
Setting lobster traps in Casco Bay. (Photo by AnnMarie Hilton/Maine Morning Star)The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear a Maine lobsterman’s legal challenge to an electronic vessel tracker requirement, putting an end to the multi-year lawsuit. 
In an order Monday, the court denied a request to take up the appeal by Frank Thompson, a Vinalhaven lobsterman. 
In a statement, Maine Department of Marine Resources Commissioner Carl Wilson said the department believes the tracking data is critically important to the long-term sustainability of the lobster fishery. 
“It will inform the lobster stock assessment, enhance offshore enforcement and support better decision-making in a range of federal management contexts,” Wilson said.
Thompson’s attorney, Matthew Gilliam with Pacific Legal Foundation, said in a statement that the denial does not diminish the importance of the issues in the suit. 
“Forcing lobstermen to carry a GPS tracker on their private boats and submit to around-the-clock surveillance as a condition of keeping their license remains a serious constitutional concern,” Gilliam said. “We are committed to fighting for Fourth Amendment protections from government overreach and we will continue to pursue every lawful avenue to protect individual rights.” 
At the center of the case is a 2023 requirement that all federally licensed lobster vessels must operate GPS trackers. The rule was passed by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, and implemented by the Maine Department of Marine Resources.
Thompson sued DMR Commissioner Carl Wilson in federal court when the rule went into effect in 2024, arguing that the tracking constituted an unreasonable search and seizure and violated his constitutional rights. 
But federal judges were not persuaded. The lawsuit was dismissed by the district court, and that ruling was upheld by the First Circuit Court of Appeals last year. With the Supreme Court declining to intervene, the First Circuit ruling is the final order in the suit. 
The Conservation Law Foundation previously filed an amicus brief in the case, supporting the regulations and arguing that it is legal and vital to track lobster boats to ensure effective management of the industry. 
“New England’s lobster population has declined dangerously,” Conservation Law Foundation Associate Attorney Sarah Shahabi said in a statement. “Tracking lobster boats provides the timely and accurate data that regulators need. This decision is a valuable step toward appropriately managing this iconic species.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont touts CT response to Medicaid cuts, stops short of pledging funds
description: CT pledged to minimize Medicaid coverage losses but stopped short of committing state funds to offset cuts passed in the 'Big Beautiful Bill.'
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont and other state officials gathered in Stamford on Monday afternoon to spotlight Connecticut’s efforts to protect residents’ Medicaid coverage in the face of pending federal changes to the program taking effect on Jan. 1.
“This is a purposeful effort by the federal government to slow things up, put in place a layer of bureaucracy, make it more complicated for people to be able to enjoy decent health care,” Lamont said. “We’re going to push back.”
Beginning Jan. 1, HUSKY D enrollees must demonstrate compliance with new work and community engagement requirements. That means proving they work at least 80 hours, or earn a minimum of $580 per month. Or they must demonstrate at least 80 hours of monthly community service or participation in a qualified training program. Though there are various exemptions.
The changes — passed as part of House Resolution 1 or the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — threaten coverage for roughly 108,000 residents enrolled in HUSKY D, the Connecticut Medicaid program for low-income adults without dependents, Department of Social Services Commissioner Andrea Barton Reeves said.
[RELATED: About 110,000 poor CT adults could lose Medicaid coverage]
The state has stepped in with funding to help fill the gap in the wake of some federal cuts, including putting up $115 million from an emergency response fund to help offset the expiration of federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans. 
But Lamont stopped short of pledging state dollars to help offset federal cuts to Medicaid.
“My first priority is what we’re doing right here. Make sure everybody that is eligible for Medicaid and SNAP take advantage of that. Before I go running to the state taxpayers, I’d like to see the feds step up and do what their piece of the responsibility is as well,” Lamont said. “We’ll figure out what the need is at the end of this year.”
In the meantime, Barton Reeves said DSS has been working to set up systems to ensure as many people as possible can be verified for eligibility through an “ex parte” process. In these cases, the state has access to data that can confirm eligibility without the enrollee having to take any action. 
DSS has also set up a website, MedicaidMattersCT.org, to help people determine whether the Medicaid changes apply to them.
The agency expects roughly two-thirds of the more than 300,000 residents with HUSKY D coverage will go through an “ex parte” verified, a spokesperson confirmed.
The Department of Social Services is also working to ensure anyone who is eligible qualifies for an exemption to the community engagement requirement based on what’s called “medical frailty.”
People can qualify as “medically frail” if they are, for example, blind, disabled or diagnosed with chronic substance use disorder or serious medical conditions, including cancer and HIV. 
Based on preliminary conversations with the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) before the release of an interim final rule on Jun. 1, state leaders believed that using medical records to prove someone had a certain diagnosis would be enough to deem them “medically frail” and exempt from work requirements.
But federal officials added another layer of complexity in the interim final rule: Instead of just proving “medical frailty,” states must also prove the condition “significantly impairs” a person from fulfilling work requirements.
“The interim final rule is still open for comment and has not been finalized by CMS, yet DSS has also identified a compliant approach that we expect will allow the vast majority of medically frail individuals to be exempted through the ex parte process,” DSS spokesperson Christine Stuart wrote in an emailed statement.
At Monday’s event, Stamford mayor Caroline Simmons and Stamford Health chief strategy officer Ben Wade discussed the HUSKY Stay Covered Task Force, a partnership between the city, the hospital and community organizations to spread the word about the Medicaid changes and help Stamford residents stay covered.
State officials applauded Stamford and pointed to the city as a model that other municipalities could emulate. 
While work requirements don’t take effect until Jan. 1, there have already been other H.R. 1-related Medicaid eligibility changes. On Oct. 1, several groups of lawfully present immigrants lost Medicaid coverage, including refugees, asylees and victims of human trafficking.

text:
Born: 05/22/1927
Indianapolis, Indiana
Died: 10/02/2026
Manchester, Vermont
Details of service:
The family plans a memorial celebration in the spring.

Marilyn Houston, 99, of Manchester, Vt. (formerly of Arlington, Vt.) died October 2, 2026. She was predeceased in 2014 by her husband, Neal J. Houston.
Marilyn was born May 22, 1927 in Indianapolis, Ind. the daughter of Elden and Florence Mills.  She spent her formative years in Forest Hills and Brooklyn, N.Y.; Westport, Mass.; and West Hartford, Ct. where her father was a Congregational Pastor.  She was a proud alumni of the University of Vermont, graduating in 1948.
Marilyn and Neal met in college and worked for the Burlington Free Press. They started their family in Burlington and then Plainfield, Vt as Neal’s career transitioned into Vermont State service. Their six children were all born in Vermont before the family moved to Alexandria, Va.  Always active and engaging, Marilyn raised her children; worked as a researcher, proofreader, and volunteer; and supported Neal’s work in Washington. At retirement, Neal and Marilyn moved to Arlington, Vt.
Throughout her life Marilyn was a lively, compelling soul. She challenged everyone she met with an intellectual curiosity that was unmatched. Her interests were wide ranging and included travel, gardening, music, tennis, bridge, reading, grammar, humor, you name it. She loved Vermont: the stone walls, and mountain landscapes, the clouds. For many years Marilyn was fulfilled by her work as a guardian-ad-litem at the Bennington District Court. Recently she enjoyed several years at Bromley Manor in Manchester developing strong friendships within the supportive community there.
Marilyn will be dearly missed by her six children:  Deborah Houston, Rebecca Moore, Laura Stewart, Neal Houston, Jr., Virginia Lima, Alison Ryan, and their respective spouses.  She also leaves 11 cherished grandchildren and eight great-grandchildren.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware tax debate sharpens as progressives gain influence
description: Meyer, Working Families Party favor higher rates on upper incomes; Ramone says Delaware should rein in spending before asking taxpayers for more DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s debate over taxes and spending is sharpening after progressive candidates scored major victories in the Democratic primary, giving greater influence to a political movement that openly suppo[...]
text:
Meyer, Working Families Party favor higher rates on upper incomes; Ramone says Delaware should rein in spending before asking taxpayers for more
DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s debate over taxes and spending is sharpening after progressive candidates scored major victories in the Democratic primary, giving greater influence to a political movement that openly supports higher income-tax rates on the state’s highest earners.  Gov. Matt Meyer has also continued to support adding new upper-income tax brackets, arguing Delaware can ask higher earners to contribute more while reducing taxes farther down the income scale.

Republican state treasurer candidate Mike Ramone is making the counterargument: Before Delaware aims at implementing a sales tax,  state leaders should first determine whether the state government’s spending is correctly targeted and delivering real results for taxpayers. 

Ramone said there have been behind-the-scenes discussions in Dover for the implementation of a sales tax for over a decade (years), and a new, more radical legislature in January might finally pull the trigger on it to keep the tax and spending express going. 
Progressives gain influence
The Sept. 15 primary strengthened the Working Families Party’s position within Democratic politics.

Working Families Party-backed candidates won one state Senate and five state House primaries. Five Democratic incumbents were among those defeated.
The results matter because the organization has a detailed economic agenda.

Its platform explicitly calls for making Delaware’s personal income tax “more progressive” by adding additional high-income brackets at increased rates.
The party also supported legislation last year that would have added tax brackets at $125,000, $250,000 and $500,000.
Meyer wants higher brackets
Meyer has made a similar argument. Delaware’s highest personal income-tax rate of 6.6% currently begins at $60,000 of taxable income.
Meyer proposed adding three higher brackets at $125,000, $250,000 and $500,000 as part of his fiscal 2026 budget proposal.

His administration argued that the change would make the system more progressive while reducing taxes for 92% of Delaware taxpayers. Under that proposal, taxpayers with taxable income below $134,667 would have faced no overall increase.

The proposal did not become law, but Meyer has continued to argue that taxpayers at substantially different income levels should not face the same top marginal rate.

The progressive argument is straightforward: If Delaware requires additional revenue to finance education, health care and other services, higher-income residents have a greater ability to absorb an increase than working- and middle-income families.
Ramone: Look at spending first

Ramone approaches Delaware’s fiscal problem from the opposite direction.

The former House minority leader and longtime small-business owner has made fiscal accountability and independent analysis of state finances central themes of his campaign for treasurer.

Ramone has said the treasurer should help taxpayers understand the economic impact of proposed taxes, fees and major spending decisions and provide an independent voice on state finances.

His broader argument is that a projected budget shortfall does not necessarily mean Delawareans are paying too little. It can also mean spending is growing too quickly.

“Every time Delaware faces a budget problem, the answer cannot simply be to go back to the people who are already paying the most and ask them for more,” Ramone said. “At some point, we have to ask why spending continues to grow, whether every program is delivering results and whether taxpayers are getting value for the money they already send to Dover.”

Ramone has previously supported directing surplus revenue toward long-term state liabilities instead of using it to support continuing expansions of government spending.

Could a sales tax be next?
Ramone said there have been behind the scenes discussions in Dover for the implementation of a sales tax for over a decade (years) and a new more radical legislature in January might finally pull the trigger on it to keep the tax and spending express going. 

He has stated publicly that officials within the Meyer administration have discussed a statewide sales tax and that such a tax could be considered if Delaware needs additional revenue.
Meyer has not publicly proposed a general sales tax, and Delaware LIVE has not independently verified that one is being developed.

That distinction is important: Higher income-tax brackets are a documented Meyer policy position. A sales tax is an option Ramone says has been discussed internally.
The Working Families Party’s published platform does not call for a general sales tax. Its tax agenda instead emphasizes collecting more revenue through higher rates on upper-income taxpayers.
A statewide sales tax would represent a much broader approach because it would reach consumers across the income spectrum.
Who should pay?
That leaves Delaware with a basic fiscal debate.

Meyer and the Working Families Party argue the state can protect most taxpayers while asking those with the greatest ability to pay to shoulder more of the cost of government.
Opponents question whether Delaware should increase its dependence on higher earners — including entrepreneurs, business owners and professionals — without first confronting the growth of state spending.

Ramone says that is the larger issue voters should consider. “Delaware families should not have to wonder which tax comes next every time state spending outgrows revenue,” Ramone said. “My approach is to promote transparency.   Help the voters understand the issues from a business and family perspective.  Let’s make government live within its means, demand accountability for the money we already collect and protect taxpayers before asking them to pay more. ”
TO GO BOX


THE DEBATE: Delaware progressives are pushing for a more progressive income-tax structure as the state faces growing spending commitments.


MEYER: The governor has proposed additional income-tax brackets at $125,000, $250,000 and $500,000 while lowering taxes for most taxpayers.


WORKING FAMILIES PARTY: Its platform explicitly supports additional high-income brackets at higher rates.


PRIMARY IMPACT: WFP-backed candidates won one Senate and five House Democratic primaries, including victories over five incumbents.


RAMONE: The Republican candidate for state treasurer argues Delaware should address spending growth, accountability and efficiency before seeking additional revenue.


SALES TAX: Ramone says Meyer administration officials have discussed a possible statewide sales tax if more revenue is needed. Meyer has not publicly proposed one, and Delaware LIVE has not independently verified those discussions.

title: Uthmeier sticks by his guns: Hope Florida transfers were ‘entirely legal, absolutely’
description: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier reiterated Monday that he considers the diversion of Medicaid funds through the Hope Florida Foundation to run political ads “entirely legal, absolutely.” He said so in answer to a reporter’s question during an unrelated news conference in Carabelle, although a state grand jury concluded the DeSantis administration had[...]
text:
James Uthmeier delivers a speech after being sworn in as state attorney general on Feb. 17, 2025, in the Florida Historic Capitol. (Photo by Jackie Llanos/Florida Phoenix)Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier reiterated Monday that he considers the diversion of Medicaid funds through the Hope Florida Foundation to run political ads “entirely legal, absolutely.”
He said so in answer to a reporter’s question during an unrelated news conference in Carabelle, although a state grand jury concluded the DeSantis administration had “misappropriated” the money in “a sophisticated scheme to fund political activities.”
“I’ve answered these questions many times before. What I’ll tell you is, while I was not the attorney general at the time that this pre-suit settlement with a nonprofit was executed, every top lawyer, virtually, in the state approved it. There’s absolutely nothing wrong with it,” he said.
Uthmeier said it’s not unusual to steer state lawsuit recoveries through nonprofits, citing Triumph Florida, which administers the state’s share of settlement money from BP following the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill, as an example.
“Protecting moms and families, and protecting kids from drug abuse, is very appropriate,” he added.
However, the Legislature created Triumph Florida through legislation signed by then-Gov. Rick Scott. Its board comprises the governor, attorney general, chief financial officer, and commissioner of agriculture.

The Phoenix’s 2026 Voter Guide 
 
Gov. Ron DeSantis elevated Uthmeier to the AG’s office following the transfer by the Hope Florida Foundation — launched by Casey DeSantis, the state’s first lady — of $10 million from a $67 million Medicaid overbilling dispute with Centene, a medical managed-care company. At the time of the transfer, Uthmeier served as DeSantis’ chief of staff.
Now he’s running for election in his own right against Democrat José Javier Rodrídguez.
Rodriguez issued a written statement in response:
